The hail was accompanied by heavy rain. Some street flooding occurred near the Grand Forks Public Library.
The hail fell at Clifford Hall on the University of North Dakota campus.

Large trees up to 8 inches in diameter were blown down across a driveway. A nearby corn crop was also flattened. The Waskish AWOS was knocked off-line due to a power outage, so its wind statistics were unavailable.
A dozen trees, about 10 to 12 inches in diameter, were blown down east of Waskish.

Multiple trees approximately 10 to 20 inches in diameter were uprooted or snapped. An old trailer was also damaged. An empty 450 gallon water tank was thrown about 100 yards over two fences and into a ditch. Crops were also damaged in the same area.
A tree, about 10 inches in diameter, was blown down across a road.
University Avenue from Columbia Road to 20th Street was flooded 18 inches deep, with water over the berms.
The funnel remained well above ground before it dissipated.
This funnel was viewed by an observer near exit 138 on Interstate 29. The funnel, located west of the interstate, was obscured by trees.

Heavy rains, mostly in the 2 to 5 inch range, fell across portions of Walsh County. There were a few reports around Lankin of 7 to 7.50 inches of rain. Overland flooding was particularly bad around Lankin, Park River, and north of Park River. Many roads were closed due to high water.
Two funnel clouds merged and lowered toward the ground. Funnels were observed from multiple locations in this area.
This funnel was seen near the junction of Interstate 29 and 32nd Avenue South in Grand Forks. The funnel was located just west of the interstate.
This tornado remained mostly over open fields and rangeland. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
Large 12 inch diameter tree limbs were broken off by the strong wind.

This tornado was viewed by the Highway Patrol just to the north of U. S. Highway 2. The tornado tracked intermittently for nearly 7 miles to about 5 miles north-northeast of Larimore. The tornado was viewed and reported by multiple sources and snapped  or uprooted numerous trees in shelterbelts. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph.

From near Forest River, a tornado tracked east-southeast to about 1.5 miles southwest of Ardoch. The tornado broke down several large tree limbs in shelterbelts and produced a fairly wide debris swirl to the west of Ardoch, as viewed by observers near the southwest edge of Ardoch. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
The hail fell along highway 81, between Grafton and Minto.
The hail fell along highway 81, between Grafton and Minto.
A tornado briefly touched down in an open field.
A brief tornado touchdown was reported north of U. S. Highway 2, heading east toward Grand Forks.
Multiple funnel clouds were reported between Reynolds and Grand Forks.
Trees were blown down at the junction of state highways 18 and 15.
Tree damage was reported along highway 81 at the Walsh/Pembina County line.
A semi tractor and trailer were blown off Interstate 29 north of Hillsboro.
The hail was accompanied by very heavy rain.
A persistent funnel produced a couple of brief touchdowns in open rangeland in southern Arne Township, near the Wells County line.
A persistent wall cloud produced a brief funnel.
Roofing material was blown off a potato warehouse on the south side of Grafton.

The tornado lifted a barn from its foundation and destroyed it while uprooting numerous trees in the farmyard. Later the tornado broke down three power poles and snapped off numerous other trees along its route. Peak winds were estimated to 105 mph.
Hail and winds to 70 mph produced widespread crop and tree damage.
The tornado snapped off numerous large tree limbs and blew down a 3000 bushel steel grain bin along its path. Peak winds were estimated at 90 mph.
The hail fell along highway 81 between Grafton and Minto.
The wind gust was measured by a ND DOT RWIS site along Interstate 29 at mile point 145.
Several trees were broken down in shelterbelts. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
The wind gust was measured by a ND DOT RWIS site along Interstate 29 near mile point 114.
A 60x120 foot diameter storage building was destroyed and roofing materials were peeled up on a potato warehouse. Several trees were snapped off. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph.
A persistent wall cloud with a funnel was reported by local fire department personnel.
Several tree limbs were broken down and a few shingles were torn off of homes. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
State highway 32 was washed out just north of the intersection with county 1. Several other washouts occurred on county roads in Elkmont and Inkster Townships.
Fields and farm roads were flooded across portions of Stavanger, Ervin, Belmont, and Bingham Townships in northeast Traill County. Several county roads were washed out or blocked by flowing water.
Fields and farm roads were flooded across northern Nash and eastern Dahlen Townships. County roads were washed out in numerous locations.
Flooding washed out portions of the railroad bed near Lankin. Street flooding and some building flooding also occurred in Lankin.
Several large 6 to 8 inch diameter tree branches were broken down in shelterbelts.
Several large 4 to 6 inch diameter tree branches were broken down in a shelterbelt. An NDAWN mesonet wind sensor nearby reported peak winds of 55 mph.
A persistent wall cloud produced a brief funnel.
The hail fell in the downtown Grand Forks area. Some melting occurred prior to the measurement, so it could have been a little larger.

Roughly three inches of rain fell in about two hours, causing some drainage problems around the city of Hankinson. Main Street was closed, as the storm sewers could not keep up with the runoff. Several businesses in low spots had minor water damage.

Several public reports, trained spotter reports, and one pilot report indicated that a series of brief funnels quickly formed and dissipated across portions of Walsh, Grand Forks, and Steele Counties. These funnels formed coincident with a band of weak rain showers which crossed the area between 230 pm and 430 pm CDT.

A series of brief funnels quickly formed and dissipated across portions of Grand Forks County. These funnels formed coincident with a band of rain showers which crossed the area between 615 pm and 715 pm CDT.

A series of brief funnels quickly formed and dissipated across portions of central Becker County. These funnels formed coincident with a band of rain showers which crossed the area between 715 pm and 815 pm CDT.
Dime to quarter sized hail damaged mature wheat fields in portions of northern Sorenson Township.
Very heavy rain fell around the Cavalier area, flooding streets and sidewalks. Some pea sized hail also fell with the rain.

Many sources around the Fargo area reported funnels on the afternoon of the 11th. All of the funnels were short lived and did not touch down. The most visible funnel was reported just west of the Fargo landfill, along 12th Avenue North.
The ground was covered with dime to quarter sized hail.
Pea to dime sized hail covered the ground.
Nickel to half dollar sized hail covered the ground.
One to two minutes of dime to nickel sizes hail ended at about 1118 AM CDT at Angle Outpost Resort.

Water rose rapidly near Manvel due to a downstream ice jam and backwater on the Turtle River. Water rose over three feet and threatened homes nearest the river, with some homes requiring emergency sandbag protection. Breakout flows from the river also flooded the golf course and overtopped highway 33 to the west of town.

The Sheyenne River rose rapidly through central portions of Lisbon, in response to an ice jam which formed near the highway 27 bridge. Flood water rose above the moderate flood stage by 11 pm CDT and eventually crested above the major flood stage. Emergency levees had been constructed in advance and emergency crews were able to contain the flooding.
A MNDOT RWIS sensor near Ottertail measured wind gusts of 58 mph.
The Hubbard County emergency manager reported portions of the southern half of Hubbard County had power lines down and two power poles snapped in half.
Power poles and trees were blown down near Sebeka and Nimrod.

Two to five inches of rain fell across portions of Kittson County, causing street flooding, basement flooding, and sewer backup in Lancaster and Hallock. Some water was reported in the Hallock courthouse. 3.48 inches of rain fell in Northcote and 3.08 inches in Hallock.
The wind gust was measured by the MNDOT RWIS sensor near St. Vincent.
The wind gust was measured by a storm chaser from Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada.
Three to seven inches of rain fell over portions of northeast Pembina County, causing street flooding, basement flooding, and sewer backup. Many fields were flooded outside of town.

Two to four inches of rain fell over portions of northwest Steele County, causing rapid rises in water levels at some locations. Two feet of water flowed over state highway 32 about six miles south of Finley. About a mile south of the junction of highways 200 and 32, three feet of water covered the road for about 70 feet.
Dime to quarter sized hail fell and most was soft graupel.
The hail was mostly half-inch size, but a few stones were larger.
Heavy rain and hail fell at the intersection of 17th Avenue South and Columbia Road.
Most of the hail was dime sized, but there were a few quarter sized stones.
Nickel to quarter sized hail fell, but melted quickly in the heavy rain.
Dime to quarter sized hail stripped leaves from trees and bean fields.
Lemon drop to quarter sized hail covered the ground.
The ground was covered by dime to half-dollar sized hail.
Dime to quarter sized hail fell near Gilby.
The report was relayed by the media.
Dime to nickel sized hail was reported.
Water covered Highway 2 near Penn.
Basement flooding was reported and water was ponded all around the farm yard.
Western Pembina Township received five to six inches of rain in a three hour period. Farm fields and access roads were flooded along highway 55.
The wind gust was estimated at 60 mph at the intersection of 34th Street and 7th Avenue Northeast in Moorhead with 1/2 mile visibility and torrential rain.
A pair of funnel clouds were spotted.
A funnel cloud was spotted in the far northeast portion of Norman County.
A funnel cloud was reported to be ascending and descending approximately halfway from the cloud base to the ground.
The rain was so heavy the observer had to pull off to the side of the road. Only a few large hailstones fell.

Intermittent tornado touchdowns occurred along this roughly 10 mile damage path. Some tree branch damage occurred though most of the path occurred over open fields. The tornado was viewed and reported by multiple spotters. Peak winds were estimated at 85 mph.
The tornado broke down several poplar trees in shelterbelts west of and adjacent to the Marshall County park and campground on the Tamarac River. Peak winds were estimated at 85 mph.
Several brief touchdowns occurred along this roughly two mile path. Peak winds were estimated at 75 mph.
Two waterspouts were sited over Lower Red Lake just north of the city of Red Lake.

This tornado tracked eastward for about a seven mile intermittent path. The tornado was viewed by aircraft and ground based observers from multiple directions. A few large tree limbs were downed in shelterbelts though the tornado was mostly over open fields. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
Branches were blown down and the steel on a shed was pealed up.
The funnel cloud was viewed from about 1 mile west of Johnston, looking north.
The hail ranged in size from 0.75 to 1.00 inch.

The tornado touched down near Grafton and tracked about six miles to the east. The tornado broke down numerous large tree limbs across the north part of Grafton and snapped off several large pine trees in the cemetery east of town. The tornado continued eastward along highway 17, severely damaging shelterbelts, tossing culvert sections, denting steel grain bins, and knocking down two power poles. Peak winds were estimated at 110 mph.

Rear flank downdraft winds from a nearby tornado pushed through the Grafton airport complex and registered at 87 knots on the midfield anemometer. One hanger received extensive damage along with five small airplanes which were parked inside.
A persistent wall cloud with a funnel was viewed as it tracked slowly east-southeastward.
A persistent wall cloud with a funnel was viewed from one mile south of Sherack as it slowly tracked east-southeastward.
The large hail was seen by a storm damage team.

The tornado tracked intermittently for about three miles, from about three miles northeast of Warren to about two miles west of Radium. One farmstead had some minor shingle damage, tree damage, and paint scarring from windborne gravel and other debris. Another farmstead had significant roof damage to a small wooden quonset due mainly to falling tree limbs. There was some tree damage in shelterbelts and minor crop scarring in fields. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph.

The tornado tracked intermittently for about eight miles, from one mile south-southwest of Key West to around eight miles north of Crookston. Large tree limbs were broken off several trees in shelterbelts and one power pole was cracked near the base. The tornado was viewed as a fairly diffuse and partially rain wrapped funnel with intermittent touchdowns and occasionally lofted debris. Peak winds were estimated at 85 mph.
A retired county sheriff reported various sizes of hail, ranging from pea to quarter to a few golfball sized stones.
Very heavy rain fell with a few large hail stones.

Street flooding occurred in Detroit Lakes. Roosevelt Avenue was barricaded due to water over the roadway, mainly on the north side of U. S. Highway 10. About 12 miles east-northeast of Detroit Lakes, rushing water washed out a culvert along highway 34. A nearby house also got water in its basement.
Water rose over state highway 64 up to six inches deep in several locations. High water was also an issue around the Lake Emma area.
Water covered county roads in the Dent area due to the heavy rainfall.
The hail fell near the intersection of Jack Pine Road and highway 9.
A large tree was blown down near the intersection of Jack Pine Road and highway 9.
Boats were overturned and docks were damaged on the northeast side of Lake Bemidji.
Two large trees were blown down at a residence along the west end of Lake Swenson.
The funnel cloud was located one mile west of the intersection of county highway 17 and state highway 46.
The funnel cloud was visible for several minutes.
Debris was captured by the KVLY tower camera in Fargo and the location was estimated.
A tornado briefly touched down near Dent.
A wall cloud with a funnel were viewed from exit 55 on Interstate 94, looking southeastward.
A wall cloud with a well defined funnel were observed just west of Interstate 94 near Pelican Lake.
Two funnel clouds were sighted by an observer two miles east of Ottertail. One funnel was about four miles east of Ottertail and the other was about one mile north of Deer Creek.
A wall cloud with a funnel nearly half way down were viewed from Deer Creek.
The hail began as pea sized but quickly got to golfball sized.
The hail was quite large, about three inches in diameter.
Minor tree damage was also reported.
The hail was quarter to half dollar size.
A tornado briefly touched down.
State radio relayed the public report of the funnel cloud sighting.
A two hundred pound grill was pushed across a deck and lawn furniture was blown about. Peak winds at Fargo Hector airport (KFAR) ranged from 45 to 57 mph for about 20 minutes.

The strong winds knocked down numerous large trees and caused widespread shingle and roof damage to homes. Large cottonwood branches of three to four inches in diameter were blown onto the top of a vehicle. Numerous sections of wooden fencing were blown down.
The spotter estimated wind speeds of 50 to 60 mph.
A spotter estimated the winds to be around 75 mph.
The winds were estimated by a trained weather spotter.
Street flooding was reported in Perham. In nearby New York Mills, 3.47 inches of rain fell.
The strong winds knocked down power lines and large trees 1.5 to 2 feet in diameter. Several sections of wooden fencing were blown down near U.S. Highway 75.
An eight inch diameter tree branch was blown down and power was out.
The wind gust was reported by a MNDOT RWIS site along Interstate 94.
The wind gust was measured by a MNDOT RWIS site on highway 78.
The wind gust was measured at the Wadena Airport.
The winds gusted from 59 to 70 mph.
The hail was mostly dime size, but a few quarter sized stones were mixed in.
The hail destroyed a personal garden.
The hail destroyed a personal garden.
The report of dime to quarter size hail came from a North Dakota Atmospheric Resources Board observer.
An ARB observer reported the penny sized hail.

The Richland County Sheriff reported a corridor from five miles west to three miles east of Wyndmere, where there were several reports of trees down in yards. There were also numerous reports of one to two inch diameter tree branches blown down across highway 13 in this region.
Heavy rains of three to five inches produced flooding in fields and across a few low lying roads.
Heavy rains of three to five inches produced runoff which inundated city sewer lift stations and flooded several basements.
Trees were blown down around the Park Rapids area and vicinity.
Several trees were blown down in a farmyard.
Dime to nickel sized hail fell for about 90 seconds.
Numerous large trees were blown down.
Small trees were blown down along with large tree branches.
Several large six to eight inch diameter tree limbs were broken down. Brief power outages were reported around the city.
Large hail and damaging winds occurred. Several large three to four inch diameter tree branches were broken down.
Hail from dime size to quarter size fell for about five minutes.
This was the second of three brief hail events through the morning.
Some tennis ball sized hail fell, but it was mostly quarter sized.
This was the third of three brief hail events of the morning.
Nickel and dime sized hail was reported.
Several sections of township roads were washed out due to heavy rains and rapid runoff along the Mahnomen and Becker county line.
Water flowed over Becker County 109 south of White Earth. Several other secondary roads near the Becker and Mahnomen county line were flooded or washed out due to the excessive rain.
The tornado knocked down a few trees in a shelterbelt and tossed road construction signs in various directions but otherwise remained largely over open fields. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
The tornado was viewed from a farm yard just west of the track as it remained over open fields. Peak winds were estimated at 75 mph.
The rotation was viewed by a spotter located southeast of Beltrami.
An evergreen was uprooted and small trees were blown down.
A large tree branch was blown down.
Dime to quarter size hail fell along with very heavy rain and strong winds.
Large hail and very heavy rain fell for about 15 minutes.
Several farm fields and farm access roads were flooded.
Fields were under water along a 30 mile stretch from Hickory Township through Thief River Falls.
Several sections of farm land were flooded by excessive rainfall. A few farm access roads were also under water.
Numerous farm fields were flooded across the central and eastern portions of Red Lake County.
Fields and farm access roads were under water in and around the greater Thief River Falls area.
Four inches of rain fell in three hours.
The Red Lake River at Highlanding rose six feet rapidly and crested near flood stage. Local fields and farm yards nearby were flooded as excessive runoff flowed into local ditches and streams.
A small metal shed was blown up onto the fencing near the cemetery.

A metal street light pole was snapped off and several trees were blown down near the courthouse area. The tornado was viewed approaching town by airport employees located two miles east-southeast of Grafton. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph.

A persistent funnel tracked just to the east of Valley City. A brief touchdown and debris cloud were viewed by employees at a city business while the funnel was still south of Interstate 94. No damage was reported as the touchdown occurred over an open field. Peak winds were estimated at 75 mph.
Ditches were flooded along a county road and briefly covered the road.
A funnel extended nearly to the ground just north of exit 294 on Interstate 94, northeast of Valley City.
A rotating wall cloud was viewed by a meteorologist located near Tower City.
Pea to penny sized hail fell.
Small marble to quarter sized hail fell near Wheatland.
Several large trees were blown down on the south end of town.
Heavy afternoon rains combined with earlier runoff to cause localized flooding near the community.
A quarter mile stretch of highway 32 was closed due to water over the road. Water was also reported to be running over Interstate 94 near the Cass County line.
Small trees and numerous large branches were blown down. Approximately 3.69 inches of rain was also reported.
Eight inch diameter tree branches were blown down.
A semi was blown over on Interstate 94 near the Casselton exit.
Two large trees were uprooted and a shed was blown down.
A large tree was blown down in a farmyard.
Several large tree limbs were broken down in the Lakewood area. Waves on Devils Lake reached nearly six feet in height and swamped several lakeshore residences.
Heavy rains in the headwaters of the Maple River produced flooding and roadbed washouts near county road 1. Area corn crops were swept away by fast moving waters.
Overland flow covered portions of North Dakota highway 32 near the Barnes County line. The golf course near Hope was also damaged by high water.
Water continued to flow over North Dakota highway 32 in multiple locations where local creeks contribute to the Maple River.
An empty steel grain bin was ripped from its pad and thrown across a farm yard. Several large tree limbs were snapped.
Several large tree limbs and a stop sign were knocked down by a burst of thunderstorm wind. Multiple reports of damage were received between Malung and Roseau.
Several large tree limbs and a street light were knocked down by thunderstorm downburst winds. Multiple damage reports were received between Wilton and Bemidji.
Strong winds occurred near the Red River bridge.

Heavy overnight rains produced rapid rises on the Pembina River and excessive runoff which overwhelmed city storm sewer pumping stations. Approximately 75 percent of homes in the community received some form of basement flooding as a result of excessive overland flow and ponding of rainwater.
Widespread overland flooding was reported around the Lancaster area. Water flowed over portions of highway 59 south of Lancaster.
A funnel cloud developed several miles south of Wahpeton, just south of the Tyler elevator complex.

This tornado touched down south of Tyler and tracked to the east for roughly 2.5 miles before crossing the Bois de Sioux River into Wilkin County, Minnesota. In Wilkin County, the tornado continued for another 2.5 miles and lifted about 650 pm CDT. The total track length was about 5 miles and peak winds were estimated at 175 mph.
This tornado touched down briefly in an open field, roughly seven miles east of a larger and much longer lasting tornado.
The persistent funnel cloud tracked east-northeast to near Foxhome before dissipating.

This tornado began in Richland County, North Dakota, at 625 pm CDT, where it had a path length of 2.5 miles. It continued in Wilkin County, Minnesota, where it finally lifted about 2.5 miles southwest of Doran. The total path length was roughly five miles and peak winds were estimated at 175 mph.

This tornado tracked for about a mile through mainly open fields. This was the latter of three distinct tornadoes which occurred from at least four distinct funnel clouds in Wilkin County during a roughly 15 to 20 minute period. Peak winds were estimated at 75 mph.

This tornado tracked intermittently for about 4 miles, mainly over open fields. However, the tornado did knock down some trees in shelterbelts and left swirls in crops. The tornado and debris cloud was viewed from near Elbow Lake. Peak winds were estimated at 90 mph.
A wall cloud and developing funnel were reported.
A brief tornado touchdown occurred in an open field. No significant damage was observed.

This tornado tracked intermittently for nearly 16 miles, to about 3 miles east of Erdahl. At this point, it continued into Douglas County. The tornado broke down numerous trees and large tree limbs along its path. At times, the tornado was wrapped in very heavy rains. Peak winds were estimated at 100 mph.
Several large tree limbs were twisted or broken down in tree stands and shelterbelts. Peak winds were estimated at 90 mph.
The hail fell one mile east of the Wadena airport.
Multiple heavy downpours of 3 to 4 inches of rain produced localized flooding of farm fields and farm access roads near the Rabbit River drainage.
Quarter sized hail was still on the ground at 6 am CDT.
A few trees were snapped off and numerous branches were taken down on Springsteel Island north of Warroad.

This tornado tracked for nearly 20 miles, about 10 miles in Towner County and 10 miles in Cavalier County. During much of this track, the tornado was likely enveloped in heavy rains and strong downburst winds with the funnel briefly visible at times. The tornado broke down two wooden power poles and numerous trees and tree limbs along its route. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph.
Ten inch diameter trees were felled and a garage was pushed off its foundation. A leg of a fertilizer plant was toppled over.
Sixteen inch diameter trees were snapped. It may have been accompanied by a funnel cloud, but it was rain wrapped and hard to see.

This tornado began in Towner County at 820 pm CDT. The tornado tracked for about 20 miles total, about 10 miles in Towner County and then about 10 miles in Cavalier County. During much of this track the tornado was likely enveloped in heavy rains and strong downburst winds with the funnel briefly visible at times. The tornado broke down two wooden power poles and numerous trees and tree limbs along its route. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph.
Rainfall amounts from 4 to 5 inches produced flooding to area fields and farm access roads.
Street flooding was reported in Egeland.

A tornado struck a farmstead in southern Grand Forks County, damaging a large well constructed equipment shed. The tornado traveled over a shelterbelt along the west edge of the property causing considerable damage. Several pieces of farm equipment were moved and flipped. An empty grain bin was removed from its foundation and lofted 300 yards, with much of the bin landing in the northwest corner of the shelterbelt.
Streets flooded in the town of Sabin. In rural areas around Sabin, ditches filled with water and flooded several rural roads.
The hail occurred 1.5 miles north of Lake Jessie in Leaf Mountain Township.
A large tree was blown down in Moorhead.
Strong east winds flipped multiple boat lifts and damaged several docks on the west end of Otter Tail Lake.
Street flooding occurred around the Fargo area from the heavy rain.
The heavy rain washed out a road north of Fort Ransom, stranding its driver.
Dime sized hail also fell.
The strong winds occurred in south Fargo.
A second round of strong winds occurred in south Fargo.
This tornado tracked for nearly seven miles, breaking numerous large tree limbs along its path. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
Several tree branches were blown down and playground equipment was toppled over.
Numerous large tree limbs were blown down throughout northern and central portions of Grand Forks.

A corridor of downburst winds developed from central East Grand Forks and extended to the east-southeast for several miles. Numerous trees were snapped off and one street light was blown down. Numerous roofs received shingle and trim damage and one metal roof was peeled off of a local print shop. Peak winds were estimated at 85 to 95 mph.
The winds were measured by a MNDOT RWIS sensor located along U. S. Highway 2.

Roads flooded from about four inches of rain in an hour and a half. The busy east-west route of 13th Avenue South was temporarily closed to traffic around the noon hour, making traffic a mess. Several basement flooding was also reported.
Large tree limbs were blown down in the northern part of town.
Several trees were blown down.
The wind speed was measured at the Fargo airport ASOS.
Three to five inches of rain fell around the Georgetown area, flooding several township roads and fields.
Multiple funnel clouds were reported.
The observer also reported 0.7 inches of rain in 15 minutes.
The hail was very jagged or had spikes.
Tree damage was noted along the four mile tornado path, with numerous branches snapped off. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
A large 18 inch diameter pine tree was snapped off.
Several large trees were blown down in shelterbelts.
Several large 8 to 10 inch diameter tree limbs were broken down in shelterbelts.
Several large trees were blown down in shelterbelts.
One or more brief funnel clouds formed along a line from near Veseleyville to near Forest River over a roughly 5 minute period.
Numerous trees were knocked down in shelterbelts over a several mile area in Prairie Centre and Walsh Centre townships.
Several large 4 to 5 inch diameter tree branches were broken down in shelterbelts.
Several trees were blown down in shelterbelts.
Several large tree limbs were broken down in shelterbelts.
Several large trees were knocked down by winds near the Minnesota State University Moorhead campus.
Several large tree limbs were knocked down in shelterbelts along U. S. Highway 10.
Rainfall amounts of 4 to 5 inches produced widespread flooding of fields and farm access roads across southern portions of Mary Township.
Strong winds gusted for 3 to 5 minutes and knocked down several large trees near Lower Rice Lake and the surrounding Rice Lake community. Heavy rains accompanied the winds.
An area of 3 to 5 inches of rain over a two hour period caused localized flooding to fields and farm access roads across southern portions of Pleasant Prairie Township.

The report was relayed by an off duty Dodge City NWS meteorologist chasing the storm. The developing funnel cloud tracked nearly due north before the initial tornado touchdown about 5 miles north-northeast of Finley around 338 PM CDT.

The tornado report was relayed by an off duty Dodge City NWS meteorologist chasing the storm. The tornado tracked northward intermittently for about 4 miles. Damage was not noticed as the tornado remained largely over open fields and rangeland. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.

The tornado tracked northward for nearly 9 miles to about 12 miles north of Mayville by 405 PM CDT and crossed into Grand Forks County. It then continued for another 8 miles to around 10 miles west of Thompson by 418 PM CDT, for a total track length of nearly 17 miles. Trees in shelterbelts and farmsteads were snapped, uprooted, or sheared off. One well constructed house near Holmes was completely swept from its foundation and destroyed. Peak winds were estimated at 185 mph. A farm shop about five and one-half miles north of Mayville was hit by the tornado, destroying the shop. A man inside survived with cuts on his hand.

This tornado began in Traill County about 3 miles north-northeast of Mayville at 349 PM CDT. The tornado crossed into Grand Forks County and tracked for an additional 8 miles to about 10 miles west of Thompson. The total track length was roughly 17 miles. One well constructed house near Holmes was completely swept from its foundation and destroyed along with several other farm buildings. Peak winds were estimated at 185 mph.

The tornado tracked northward for about a mile to about 1 mile west-southwest of the Baldhill Dam. The tornado snapped a wooden power pole, knocked down several poplar trees, and shredded a portion of an old corn field. Peak winds were estimated at 100 mph.

Multiple funnel clouds were viewed to the west, southwest, and south of Dazey, all moving northward. One produced a brief touchdown in an open field near Dazey, though no damage was observed. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
Numerous large trees were blown down or snapped in farmsteads by thunderstorm forward flank downdraft winds.
Numerous trees were blown down in shelterbelts.
The tornado tracked northward over open rangeland for about a mile and then it crossed into Benson County about 8 miles west of Warwick at 428 PM CDT. Peak winds were estimated at 70 mph.
The tornado began in Eddy County about 11 miles east of Sheyenne at 427 PM CDT. The tornado crossed into Benson County and dissipated over open pastureland. Peak winds were estimated at 70 mph.

The tornado tracked northward for nearly 7 miles, to around 1 mile north of Blabon. The tornado produced severe tree damage in field and farm shelterbelts located along its path. Rear flank downdraft winds also produced tree damage at the Hope golf course. Peak winds were estimated at 120 mph.

The tornado tracked northward intermittently for nearly 7 miles. Trees were damaged in shelterbelts and farm yards. A center pivot irrigation system was tumbled and twisted near Colgate. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph.

The tornado tracked northward intermittently for about 7 miles. A pole barn and several farm outbuildings were destroyed. Large trees were snapped or uprooted. Debris was thrown near Emerado and just east of the Grand Forks Air Force Base. Peak winds were estimated at 120 mph.

The tornado tracked northeastward for nearly 3 miles to around 8 miles east-northeast of Hope. Numerous trees were severely damaged in shelterbelts. An abandoned farmhouse was collapsed and other farm buildings were damaged. Peak winds were estimated at 125 mph.

Observers at the Grand Forks International Airport reported a wall cloud south of the airport complex moving north. Subsequent reports indicated a tornado passing near the airport from 2147Z to 2151Z. Peak winds at the airport reached 48 knots as the tornado passed west of the airport.

The tornado touched down just west of the Grand Forks International Airport and tracked northward for nearly 10 miles. The tornado did lift briefly around 501 PM CDT before reforming with two tornadic vortices extending from a common wall cloud. The twin tornadoes then tracked cyclically up to a mile apart while they snapped and uprooted trees in shelterbelts and collapsed a pole barn. Peak winds were estimated at 100 mph.

The tornado tracked for about 2 miles to near 5 miles south-southeast of Northwood. The tornado was viewed by spotters near Golden Lake and the town of Hatton. Several tree tops were snapped along the Goose River. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
The tornado tracked northeastward intermittently for about 3 miles. Several large branches and tree limbs were knocked down in shelterbelts. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.

A funnel cloud was observed forming to the north of the Interstate 29 exit west of Oslo, Minnesota, at 518 PM CDT. The tornado tracked for nearly a mile before crossing the Red River and continuing into Minnesota about 5 miles north of Oslo, Marshall County. The tornado continued for another 4 miles in Minnesota, ending by 529 PM CDT. Several large trees were snapped near the river. Peak winds were estimated at 90 mph.
The tornado tracked northward over open fields for about a mile. Some large tree limbs were broken down in a shelterbelt. Peak winds were estimated at 75 mph.

The tornado produced intermittent touchdowns along a nearly 8 mile north-northeast track. The dissipating funnel was visible passing south of Grand Forks through 545 PM CDT. Large tree branches were broken down in field shelterbelts and near homes in Merrifield. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
The wind gust was measured by the Grand Forks International Airport ASOS.
The tornado tracked northward intermittently for about two miles. No damage was detected as the tornado stayed largely over open fields. Peak winds were estimated at 75 mph.
The hail was reported in the 2239Z observation at the Grand Forks International Airport.
The tornado tracked northward for about 2 miles. Trees were snapped or uprooted in shelterbelts. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph.
The tornado tracked northward for about 4 miles. Several large trees were snapped or uprooted in shelterbelts. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph.
The tornado tracked northeast for about 1 mile. Several tree limbs were snapped off in a country cemetery south of Fossum. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.

This tornado began in Douglas County, Minnesota. It moved northward into Otter Tail County and produced an additional 38 miles of continuous damage path. The tornado destroyed numerous homes and farmsteads along its path, completely sweeping 7 homes from their foundations. At times, this multi-vortex tornado complex consisted of multiple tornadic tubes pivoting around a common center. Peak winds were estimated at 175 mph.

Two persistent wall clouds tracked with periodic funnels from north central Otter Tail County into south central Becker County. One produced a brief tornadic touchdown near Rose Lake in Hobart Township. Peak winds were estimated at 75 mph.
Golf ball to hen egg sized hail fell.

The tornado tracked northeastward for roughly 4 miles, where it then crossed into Polk County at 407 PM CDT. The tornado continued in Polk County for another 2 miles. Several trees were knocked down in farm shelterbelts. The total track length was about 6 miles with peak winds estimated at 80 mph.

This tornado began in Mahnomen County about 3 miles east of Bejou at 400 PM CDT. It crossed into Polk County and tracked for another 2 miles, giving a total track length of about 6 miles. The tornado knocked down several trees in farm shelterbelts. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
Funnels were viewed both northwest and southwest of Fosston, moving to the north-northeast.

This tornado tracked north-northeastward for roughly a mile, across portions of Long Lost Lake. Numerous large tree limbs were knocked down and large trees were snapped. Peak winds were estimated at 90 mph.

This tornado tracked nearly due north for about 3 miles. The tornado knocked down numerous large tree limbs and uprooted or snapped off several trees. Some shingles, gutters, and trim pieces were torn off of a house. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph.

This tornado touched down in Otter Tail County and tracked northeastward for about 2 miles before crossing into Wadena County just southwest of the Wadena city limits. The tornado developed rapidly into a multi-vortex wedge type tornado as it approached Wadena. The tornado continued in Wadena County another 8 miles and ended about 516 PM CDT. Otter Tail County received mainly extreme tree damage with peak winds estimated at 170 mph.

This multi-vortex wedge tornado began in Otter Tail County about 3 miles southwest of the city of Wadena at 459 PM CDT. It tracked for about 2 miles in Otter Tail County, then it continued for another 8 miles in Wadena County. The tornado ravaged the western half of the community of Wadena. Numerous homes were flattened to the ground and at least one was completely swept from its foundation and destroyed. Public and industrial buildings were wrecked, the fairgrounds were damaged, and headstones in the cemetery were overturned. School buses and vehicles were propelled through the air for hundreds of yards. The tornado hit on the day of the Wadena all-school reunion, so many additional people were in the area. Roughly 100 people were displaced from their homes. Peak winds were estimated at 170 mph.

The tornado tracked northward intermittently for roughly 2 miles. The tornado knocked down several large tree limbs and snapped off some smaller trees. Heavy farm machinery was moved around by the winds. Peak winds were estimated at 90 mph.

The tornado tracked northeast for roughly 6 miles. The tornado knocked down numerous large tree limbs and snapped or uprooted several large trees from the southeast edge of Itasca State Park, across portions of Beauty Lake, and Lake Alice. Peak winds were estimated at 100 mph.

This tornado began in Walsh County, North Dakota, about 4 miles north-northwest of Oslo, Minnesota, at 521 PM CDT. It crossed the Red River into Minnesota about 5 miles north of Oslo. The tornado continued to track northeastward for about 4 miles. Numerous large tree limbs were knocked down and several trees were snapped in shelterbelts. Peak winds were estimated at 90 mph.
The tornado tracked northward for roughly a mile. Several large trees were knocked down onto power lines and one power pole was snapped along highway 92. Peak winds were estimated at 100 mph.

The tornado tracked east-northeastward intermittently for about 5 miles, where it reached the Cass County line east of Nimrod. The tornado continued northeast into Cass County for several more miles. Numerous large tree branches were broken down along this path. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
This tornado tracked northeastward intermittently for roughly 4 miles. The tornado knocked down several large tree branches along its route. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
The tornado tracked northeastward for about a mile against the west end of Lake Kabekona. Several large branches were broken down along its path. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.

A well defined tornado was viewed by an off duty SPC meteorologist. The tornado tracked northward intermittently for roughly 7 miles. The tornado snapped or uprooted numerous trees in shelterbelts and damaged farm buildings near the Fisher/Nesbit township border. Peak winds were estimated at 100 mph.

The tornado tracked northward for roughly 3 miles along the Marshall and Beltrami county line, before crossing into Roseau County just south of Skime. The tornado continued northeastward into Roseau County for about one mile and lifted about 1 mile east of Skime. Several large trees were knocked down or snapped along the tornado path. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph.

This tornado began in Marshall County about 11 miles north of Grygla at 554 PM CDT. The tornado continued into Roseau County and tracked northeastward for roughly a mile. Several large trees were knocked down or snapped along the tornado path. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph.

This tornado tracked northeastward for nearly 3 miles. The tornado tore a 5,000 bushel steel grain bin from its concrete pad and tossed it a half mile into a field. Several trees were snapped off or uprooted in a shelterbelt and shingles were torn from a house roof. Peak winds were estimated at 90 mph.

This tornado tracked northward for roughly 2 miles. Several large tree limbs were knocked down in shelterbelts along the tornado path. One farmstead received minor shingle damage. Peak winds were estimated at 85 mph.

This tornado began in Polk County and tracked northeastward for nine miles to the Red Lake County line about 5 miles north-northeast of Mentor. After crossing into Red Lake County, it continued for an additional 6 miles. The tornado tracked across Maple Lake and the community of Mentor. Trees were sheared off or uprooted, power poles were snapped, and roofs and garages were destroyed. A convenience store and gas station along U. S. Highway 2 were flattened. Cabins, campers, boats, and docks were damaged along the northeast side of Maple Lake. Peak winds were estimated at 145 mph.

This tornado began in Polk County, about 4 miles south-southwest of Mentor at 615 PM CDT. The tornado tracked into Red Lake County and continued an additional 6 miles to roughly 4 miles east-northeast of Terrebonne. The tornado sheared trees and blew down farm buildings near the Polk County line and lofted debris from Mentor well past the community of Plummer. The total track length was about 15 miles and peak winds were estimated at 145 mph.
This tornado tracked northeastward for roughly 2 miles. The tornado blew a parked semi tractor-trailer rig off the highway and injured the driver. Peak winds were estimated at 90 mph.
Numerous large tree branches were broken down and several trees were uprooted by violent wind bursts. The winds were accompanied by a steady downpour of rain.

This tornado tracked for roughly 7 miles, snapping off numerous trees in shelterbelts along its path. The roof was torn off a small shed near Old Mill State Park and some row crops showed ground scouring. Peak winds were estimated at 105 mph.
Areas of 4 to 5 inches of rainfall produced flash flooding in fields and farm access roads in southern Normania Township.
A rapid 2 to 3 inch downburst of rain produced street flooding in Lakota. Water spread a foot or more deep across several streets and stretched from sidewalk to sidewalk.
Several large tree branches and tree limbs were blown down. A sliding door was blown off a grainery.
Dime to quarter sized hail fell with very strong winds.
Several large tree branches and tree limbs were broken down.
The tornado tracked east-southeastward intermittently for about 3 miles. Several large tree branches and limbs were blown down in shelterbelts along the track. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.

This tornado tracked eastward just south of the Park River and crossed Interstate 29 near milepost 178. No significant damage was observed in fields. Spotters reported that this tornado lifted before crossing the Red River and that a second tornado formed several minutes later further east into Minnesota. Peak winds estimated at 75 mph.
The wind gust was measured by a MNDOT RWIS mesonet sensor.

This tornado tracked briefly to the north-northeast before a wet rear-flank downdraft overtook it as viewed and recorded by multiple storm chase teams. A second and more powerful tornado eventually formed from the parent supercell thunderstorm and impacted the the community of Wadena.  Very heavy rains and damaging downdraft winds obscured the overall tornado path.  However large tree limbs were broken down and smaller trees were uprooted by the event suggesting peak winds to 90 mph.
This tornado tracked intermittently for about 3 miles, mainly over open fields and pasture. Some larger branches were broken off in a shelter belt.  peak winds estimated to 80 mph.
Two foot diameter trees were uprooted.
Trees were blown down onto powerlines, resulting in power outages.
A new grain bin was dented to a depth of three to four feet.

Several grain bins were lofted for a mile or more and destroyed. Large pine trees were uprooted and numerous trees were stripped of leaves and branches. Equipment storage buildings were unroofed and otherwise flattened to the ground.  The tornado tracked continuously for at 14 to 15 miles. There was also widespread wind and hail damage observed in the area.
Damage occurred along the Barnes and Griggs county line.
Strong winds were reported at Horace.
The strong winds were measured at the corner of University Avenue and 32nd avenue south in Fargo.
The wind gust was measured by an ND DOT RWIS sensor near Buffalo.
The wind speeds were estimated.

Downburst winds raked across portions of western Roseau County.  Numerous trees were knocked down across portions of Polonia and Barto Townships.  Several farmsteads had tree and roofing damage. Some forested areas saw 1 of every 4 trees knocked down.
The west-northwest wind gust was measured by the Hallock AWOS.
Nickel to quarter size hail fell.
Several small to medium sized trees were blown down.
Strong winds occurred at Vergas.

Significant tree damage occurred at three farmsteads with debris thrown in divergent patterns. Peak winds were estimated to 105 mph. Significant crop damage occurred across southern Davenport township due to additional widepsread damaging winds and large hail.
Street flooding was caused by 4.25 inches of rain.
Four to five inches of rain fell, flooding a yard.
Nearly three inches of rain fell, causing flooding in low spots. Local sloughs and creeks also filled with water and overspilled their banks.
The hail ranged in size from 0.88 to 1.25 inches.
There was also well defined rotation overhead.
A small ride at the Clay County fair was damaged due to strong winds.
Tree branches up to 4 inches in diameter were snapped.
A large tree was blown down next to the firehouse. A lot of smaller branches were also blown off trees around town.
The wind gust was measured by a MNDOT RWIS sensor.
Roughly 1.50 inches of rain fell in 15 minutes.
A flooded basement was reported.
Numerous large tree limbs were broken off in shelter belts near Interstate 94 and in treed areas bordering the northwest corner of Pelican Lake.
A brief tornado touchdown was viewed in the open fields about one mile west of the Wadena Airport (KADC).  Maximum winds speed were estimated to 80 mph.

The tornado tracked nearly due eastward along ND Highway 46 with occassional movement back and forth across the highway.  Mature shelter belts that lined the highway were violently shattered at various points along the route indicating peak winds of 100 to 110 mph. Large hail, heavy rains, and damaging downburst winds accompanied the tornado.
A persistent wall cloud with multiple funnels was viewed passing east of Nome. One or more of the funnels touched down briefly in mainly opened fields.
This tornado knocked down several large tree limbs and a few smaller trees in farm shelter belts along its path. peak winds are estimated to 85 mph.
Peak gust measured at the NDAWN winds sensor near ND Highway 46.  Numerous large tree limbs were blown down in shelter belts along Highway 46 and in farmsteads and communities near the highway.

This tornado was embedded in a squall line which also produced large hail and a wide swath of damaging downburst winds. the most extreme tornado damage was observed at two farmsteads northwest of elliot and in the town of elliot where wooden quonset structures and large steel grain bins were violently crumpled and tossed in various directions. Peak winds estimated to 105 mph.
Numerous large tree limbs were broken down around the community.

This tornado was embedded in a squall line which also produced large hail and a wide swath of damaging downburst winds. The most extreme tornado damage was observed at two farmsteads, one about four miles west of Lisbon where a barn was ripped off its foundation and destroyed, and another about 4 miles ESE of Lisbon where a well constructed steel shop was completely blown apart. At least three wooden power poles were snapped at two different locations east of Lisbon. Numerous lareg trees were blown down or uprooted in Lisbon, and many homes and business had extensive roofing damage. peak winds estimated to 120 mph.

A Squall Line with damaging downburst winds raked across West Fargo and into Fargo through the early morning hours. Winds flipped over two semi trailors parked near the fair grounds and completly tore off a large metal section of city garbage transfer station along U.S. Highway 10. Industrial business roofing damage and the movement of small machinery items in various lots indicated the occurence of one or more small surface eddies in the overall downburst pattern.
And old barn collapsed and the back end of a pole shed was blown off by damaging downburst winds.
This was the third severe thunderstorm to affect the area during a 12 hour period.
Winds measured at the NDAWN sensor located one half mile south of the airport sensor measured a peak wind to 58 mph.

Numerous large trees were snapped or uprooted at various locations along a roughly 3 mile wide path centered along MN Highway 210. Farm machinery was moved about, doors and roofing materials were torn off farm buildings and homes. Peak winds estimated at 90 to 100 mph at multiple locations.

This tornado was enshrouded in heavy rain, large hail, and damaging downburst winds. Numerous large trees were knocked down or uprooted along this path. At least 6 wooden power poles were snapped off. One farmstead lost a section of a large pole shed. A nearby farmstead had a concrete silo toppled. This tornado crossed part of the damage field from a larger June 17th tornado north of Bluffton in Bluffton Township.

This tornado mainly affected portions of Lyons State Forest. Several poplar trees were snapped or blown down across CR 26. A damage path was evident further back into the trees on both sides of the county road, but access to view additional damage away from the road was not possible due to poor road conditions and high water. Peak winds were estimated from 75 to 80 mph.
Several Large tree limbs were broken down in shelter belts near U.S. Highway 10.
Downburst winds of from 50 to 60 mph occurred ahead of and concurrent with a  squall line.
Large tree limbs were broken down and small wind driven hail raked flower beds. hail sized estimated at dime to nickel sized.
Hail ranged from dime to quarter sized.
Hail fell for 10 minutes at Camp Wilderness.
Also large tree branches of 4-6 inch diameter were broken off.
Hail ranging from 2 to 4 inch diameter fell in an area between Sebeka and Blue Grass. Hail punched large holes through a steel shop roof and broke out several windows.
A brief touchdown occurred in an open field north of U.S. Highway 10.
This tornado touched down near Hwy 71 and had an intermittent path to the east.  Several smaller branches were broken down in forested areas along the path.
A waterspout formed on the north side of little Pine Lake but dissipated as it came to shore.  A persistent wall cloud was viewed for several minutes by spotters in the Perham area.
A funnel was viewed near the Douglas County line.
Peak wind measured at the Hampden RAWS sensor.
Peak wind measured by the Hampden RAWS sensor near the Ramsey County line.
Tornado tracked intermittently for about 5 miles over mainly open rangeland. Tornado was enshrouded in damaging downburst winds and very heavy rains. Peak winds were estimated to 85 mph.

Widespread downburst wind damage was noted across southeast Griggs County and into adjacent portions of southwest Steele County and northeast Barnes County.  Significant crop and tree damage occurred across the southern half of Broadview Township which indicated peak wind speeds of from 90 to 100 mph.

Widespread downburst wind damage was noted across southwest Steele County and into adjacent portions of southeast Griggs County and northeast Barnes County.  Significant crop and tree damage occurred across the southern half of Willow Lake  Township which indicated peak wind speeds of from 90 to 100 mph.

Widespread downburst wind damage was noted across northeast Barnes County and into adjacent portions of southwest Steele County and southeast Griggs County.  Significant crop and tree damage occurred across Baldwin Township which indicated peak wind speeds of from 90 to 100 mph. This damage is separate from concurrent and adjacent tornado damage.
Two funnels were observed in the Star Lake area. One produced a brief touchdown but no apparent damage.

Richland County dispatch relayed a public report of a tornado touchdown about 1 mile south of Geneseo in Sargent County.  The tornado tracked east for about 1 mile and the crossed into Richland County around 836 pm CDT where it continued for about 1 more mile before lifting around 838 pm CDT.  No significant damage was reported as the tornado stayed over mainly opened fields.

This tornado began in Sargent County at 834 pm CDTcdt, where it had an approximate 1 mile path.  It continued in Richland County for about one additional mile, for a total path length of about 2 miles. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
Two hunters died after the boat the were using capsized on a flooded portion of the Maple River in Hill Township, about 37 miles west of Fargo.
A 73 year old resident of Oakport Township suffered a heart attack and died while he and his family were filling and placing sandbags to protect their home, located north of Moorhead.
After the storm passed there were drifts of hail several inches deep in one yard.
The large hail broke windows on a car.

The hail fell about eight miles south of Bagley.
The hail fell two miles south and 1.25 miles west of Felton.

Sustained winds above 40 mph, with gusts up to 55 mph, occurred across Wilkin County between Breckenridge and Rothsay, blowing down many large tree branches. In Breckenridge, a few two foot diameter trees were also blown down. The MNDOT RWIS site near Rothsay recorded a peak wind of 55 mph at 534 am CST.

Sustained winds above 40 mph, with gusts to 59 mph, affected portions of eastern Otter Tail County, breaking off many large tree branches. A peak wind of 59 mph was measured at the Fergus Falls airport at 553 am CST.
A wind gust of 58 mph was measured at the Langdon AWOS.

Law enforcement observed this tornado as it tracked intermittently along a roughly 4 mile track. The wall cloud structure and storm continued northeastward and produced at least one additional brief tornado. Peak winds were estimated at 75 mph.

There were reports of damage to many cars and buildings in Walcott.  The firehall and city administration building lost sections of roofing and falling tree limbs crushed vehicles and roofs of several homes.
Tree and fence damage occurred all over Fargo.

Large trees and fences were blown down all over West Fargo. Power outages were also reported.

Numerous trees were blown down in farmsteads and communities across western Norman County.  In Halstad and Ada, broken tree limbs crushed vehicles and severly damaged roofing on numerous homes.

A roof was blown off a building.
There were many reports of damage around Crookston, with many trees, power lines, and street signs blown over. A small shed was blown down and falling tree limbs damaged the roofs of numerous homes.

Several roads were overtopped with water and there were also reports of flooded basements.
A tree was blown down on county road 22 north of Bemidji.

Many large tree branches were blown down.
Cattle pens were damaged and a large tank was blown across the road.

Large tree branches were blown down around town. A 58 mph wind gust was measured at the Cavalier AWOS.

A MNDOT RWIS sensor at St. Vincent reported 57 mph wind gusts, which blew down numerous large tree branches.

The tornado broke down two power poles along the west side of highway 281 and severely damaged several trees in a shelterbelt east of highway 281. Peak winds were estimated at 105 mph.
This tornado tracked intermittently along the path and knocked down several trees in shelterbelts. Peak winds were estimated at 85 mph.
Trees and limbs were blown down along the tornado path. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.

A sequence of two short lived funnels was viewed from near Wheatland. The funnels appeared to come down about one-third of the way from the cloud and then go back up again. From this distance, these funnels likely produced the brief tornado touchdown three miles south of Ayr.
A well developed wall cloud with a weak funnel were reported.
Very high winds were reported east of Gwinner along with near zero visibility due to wind and rain. The highway had several tree branches across it.

Large trees were blown down in north Bemidji. Street flooding was also reported.

Trees were blown down in Northwood.
Several large 3 to 5 inch diameter tree branches were blown down. Large portions of small grain and corn crops were lodged by the winds across northeast Michigan and northern Americus townships.
Very heavy rains and strong winds were accompanied by a few dime to nickel sized hail.
A few large 3 to 5 inch diameter tree branches were broken down and area small grain and corn crops were partially lodged across southern Bygland township.

Several houses lost shingles or had siding or roofing damages. Numerous large trees and tree limbs were broken down around town. Widespread wind damage was evident throughout Bowen and Forman townships.

Numerous large tree limbs were broken down around town. A center pivot irrigation system four miles west of town was flipped. Widespread wind damage was evident throughout Harlem and Sargent townships.
Tin roofing was blown off a machine shop and large tree limbs were broken down. Widespread wind damage was evident throughout Taylor Township.
A roof was torn off a steel grain bin. Numerous large tree limbs were broken down. Widespread wind damage was evident throughout Weber and Rutland townships.
The funnel cloud location was approximated by a spotter who was located three miles east of Gwinner.
Large tree branches were blown down.
Several large tree branches and a few large tree limbs were broken down around Lidgerwood. Peak winds were estimated at 60 to 70 mph across Grant and Moran townships.

Several grain bins were dented in and numerous large tree limbs were broken down at a farmstead. Numerous tree branches were broken down in shelterbelts throughout Devillo and Lemars townships. Some corn fields were flattened.

The wind gust was measured by a NDSU NDAWN mesonet site. Numerous large tree limbs were broken down around the town of Wyndmere along with four wooden power poles. Wind damage was widespread throughout Wyndmere and Danton townships suggestive of peak winds from 55 to 65 mph, with isolated peak winds to 80 mph.

This tornado was first reported by an observer located south of Sutton and looking east towards Hannaford. The tornado snapped down several trees in a shelterbelt and flattened part of a corn field before lifting. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph.

This tornado tracked into the northern portion of Long Lake and became quite visible as it pulled up lake water. The tornado tracked for roughly 3 miles and became rain wrapped. Peak winds were estimated at 75 mph.
The tornado briefly touched down in an open field. Peak winds were estimated at 70 mph.

The tornado knocked down several trees in various shelterbelts along its route. At one farmstead several sheets of steel roofing were ripped up and tossed off of a shed and numerous tree branches were scattered about. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph.

This tornado developed over the west bay of Devils Lake and tracked intermittently across open lake water for nearly three miles. The tornado was partially rain wrapped but briefly viewable from Lakewood Park. Peak winds were estimated at 75 mph.

Numerous large tree limbs were broken down around Greenbush. Trees were blown down on cars and roofs of homes. Power lines were also downed. The county highway department building was severely damaged. Equipment in the building was also damaged. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph based on extreme structural damage and related tree damage. Trees and power lines were down all around Karlstad.

Several large three foot diameter trees were broken down in Badger. A wooden storage shed at the cemetery was torn off its foundation and flipped over.

Water flowed over several sections of county and township roads in southern and central Harmony township. Numerous farm access roads and fields were flooded.

Quarter to half dollar sized hail fell. Wind drive hail produced crop, roofing, and some vehicle damage across neche township.
Tree branches up to 4 inches in diameter were blown down.

This tornado tracked for a distance of nearly four miles, to around four miles south-southwest of Grandin. Initially the tornado tracked southward for about 1.5 miles before turning southeast. Farm shelterbelts along the route had numerous large tree branches and tree limbs broken down. The long rope tornado was partially obscured in heavy rains at times. Peak winds were estimated at 85 mph.

This tornado tracked southeastward for nearly three miles to around three miles northwest of Mapleton. The tornado took down three sets of wooden high voltage double power poles. It continued into a farmyard and completely removed the roof from one farmhouse and blew apart the attached garage. A semi tractor and trailer in the yard were rolled. Numerous trees were snapped or uprooted and smaller sheds were destroyed. Peak winds were estimated at 130 mph.

Two to three inches of heavy rain produced street flooding in the community of Comstock, in nearby farm fields, and across several sections of road in western Holy Cross township. Flooding conditions along adjacent portions of the Red River were also increased.

Heavy rains of 2 to 4 inches fell across portions of Walcott township. Street flooding occurred in the community of Walcott, while several sections of farmland and portions of local roads were inundated.

A persistent wall cloud and funnel tracked northeast from the Baldhill Dam area and produced multiple brief touchdowns along its path. Peak winds were estimated at 70 mph.

This tornado tracked north northeastward for roughly two miles before crossing into Cass County. The tornado was likely enshrouded in downburst winds and heavy rain. The tornado and accompanying winds knocked down numerous wooden power poles along its path and four steel t-bar high voltage towers. Peak winds were estimated at 120 mph.

This tornado originated in Richland County about four miles north of Walcott at 846 pm CDT. The tornado was likely enshrouded in downburst winds and heavy rains. The tornado crossed North Dakota highway 46 and continued to break down several single and double pole wooden power towers in southwest Pleasant township. Peak winds were estimated at 120 mph.

This tornado tracked for about two miles to the north-northeast and was likely enshrouded in downburst winds and heavy rains. The tornado flipped a parked semi trailer and tore out two large 40,000 bushel steel grain bins at one farmstead and spread debris downwind for a mile. Several trees were toppled onto rooftops in the community of St. Benedict. Peak winds were estimated at 100 mph.

This tornado tracked northward for about four miles and lifted near the Woodhaven Park in southwest Fargo. The tornado was likely enshrouded in downburst winds and heavy rain as it knocked down several wooden power poles and two metal truss power towers along its path. Sections of roofing were torn off of two apartment buildings. Many residences had tree, vehicle and roof damage. Peak wind were estimated at 135 mph.

This tornado tracked north-northeastward along the eastern edge of Moorhead and was likely enshrouded in downburst winds and heavy rain. A few wooden power poles were snapped and numerous trees were uprooted or snapped. Some mature trees were thrown more than 100 feet. Peak winds were estimated at 105 mph.

This tornado tracked intermittently to the northeast for about nine miles. A 30x40 foot wooden shed was completely blown off its foundation and destroyed in one farmyard. Numerous trees were snapped in shelterbelts along its path. Peak winds were estimated at 105 mph.

This tornado tracked for about six miles and was likely enshrouded in downburst winds and heavy rain along much of its path. Several sections of center pivot irrigation systems were flipped.
