The strong wind gusts were measured by a MNDOT RWIS site.
The hail still covered the ground 30 minutes after it fell.
The time was estimated from radar.
Several 5 to 6 inch diameter tree branches were blown down.
Trees were uprooted in Fort Totten.
A flag pole and tree branches were blown down. The thunderstorms also dropped 1.50 inches of rain.
More than 20 to 25 trees were uprooted in Hope. Three trees landed on cars and two trees landed on homes. The grain elevator was also damaged.
The wind gust was measured at the Cooperstown airport.
A grain bin was damaged near Hope.
Strong winds damaged a farmstead at Galesburg. A large steel gas tank was blown off its moorings.
Numerous 6 to 10 inch diameter tree branches were blown down.
A large tree was split in two from strong winds.
Several trees in a shelterbelt were blown down.
Many large tree branches were blown down by the strong wind. Crops were also flattened by the wind and rain.
An observer reported 3.50 inches of rain early in the morning of the 1st.
The wind gust was measured by a MNDOT RWIS sensor northwest of Rothsay. Stronger wind gusts may have occurred shortly after, but the power failed.
Three to six inches of rain fell over the Hope area, causing street and basement flooding. Numerous county and local township roads were flooded across Willow Lake and Carpenter townships.
After the 3 to 6 inches of rain fell over the Hope area, overland flooding kept numerous roads closed.
The funnel lasted for two to three minutes.
The funnel was observed just south of Luverne.
A stop light and several trees were blown down.
A 60 foot tall pine tree was blown down.
The hail fell intermittently over a five minute period.
Trees were blown down onto power lines.
Numerous large branches were broken off trees across several shelterbelts in Dahlen Township.

This tornado tracked intermittently for about 26 total miles, while wrapped in heavy rain and downburst winds. About sixteen of the miles occurred in Walsh County with about ten miles in Pembina County. The tornado touched down near Pleasant Valley, passed near Homme Dam, then crossed into Pembina County about one mile northwest of Hoople. The tornado snapped or uprooted numerous trees and tore a roof off of a pole barn. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph.

This tornado began in Walsh County, about six miles west-southwest of Park River.  The tornado tracked intermittently for about 26 total miles, while wrapped in heavy rain and downburst winds. About ten of the miles occurred in Pembina County, while about sixteen of the miles occurred in Walsh County. Numerous trees were either snapped or uprooted along its track. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph.
The hail fell off and on for about five minutes.
Sustained winds above 40 mph, with gusts to 55 mph, were reported between Mooreton and Wahpeton, downing numerous large tree branches. The peak wind at the Wahpeton airport was 55 mph at 455 am CST.
Sustained winds above 40 mph, with gusts to 55 mph, affected portions of northern Grant County from Wendell to Ashby, downing many large tree branches.
Sustained winds above 40 mph, with gusts to 55 mph, affected portions of eastern Otter Tail County from Battle Lake to Urbank, downing many large tree branches.
A funnel cloud was spotted near the Ransom County line northwest of Englevale.
A persistent wall cloud was reported along with a funnel extending about half way down to the ground.
The wind gust was measured at a NDAWN mesonet site.
The wind gust was measured at a NDAWN mesonet site.
Several sections of farmland and farm access roads were flooded across Rochester Township.
Several sections of farmland and farm access roads were flooded across portions of Sverdrup and Broadview townships.
Overland flooding continued northwest of Page after 3 to 6 inches of rain fell.
Overland flooding continued east and southeast of Cooperstown after 3 to 6 inches of rain fell.
State highway 32 was closed to traffic both north and south of Finley due to water overtopping the roadway. The sheriff reported that many sections of county roads were washed out.
Overland flooding continued near Pillsbury after three to six inches of rain fell.
Several sections of farmland and farm access roads were flooded across Ellsbury Township.
Overland flooding continued around Finley after 3 to 6 inches of rain fell.
A few large tree branches were blown down in a farm shelterbelt northeast of Rothsay in Trondhjem Township.
A few large 6 to 8 inch diameter tree limbs were blown down and a part of a corn field was flattened.
Pea to dime sized hail fell southwest of Hillsboro.

Brief but very heavy rain mixed with strong winds and hail to bring all lanes of traffic to a stop along Interstate 29 near mile post 100. Traffic was able to resume after about a 10 to 15 minute period. Heavy rain fell over a roughly 20 minute period. A nearby NDAWN mesonet site measured peak winds to 48 mph and 1.07 inches of rain during the period.
Pea to nickel sized hail fell on the south side of Grand Forks.
About five inches of rain fell over a three hour period.
Quarter to half dollar sized hail fell near Walmart in south Grand Forks.
A 12 inch diameter tree was snapped at the root at the corner of 28th avenue and Oak Street.
Quarter to walnut sized hail fell for a few minutes.
Torrential rains fell along with numerous nickel to walnut sized hail. The hail began small but increased in size later on.
The observer also measured 3.30 inches of rain during the storm.
Nickel to quarter sized hail caused some crop damage.
A few walnut sized hail fell.
The observer reported 2.75 inches of rain.
About 3.50 inches of rain fell over the course of about 45 minutes.
The observer reported 1.82 inches of rain over a two hour period.
The winds were measured at Hector Airport on the north end of Fargo.
The observer measured 3.00 inches of rain over a two hour period.
The thunderstorms dropped 4.70 inches of rain in about two hours.
Lots of 0.50 to 0.75 inch hail fell.
The occupants of a house heard the hail hitting the side of the house and woke up.
Mainly dime to nickel sized hail fell along with a few quarter sized hailstones.
Quite a bit of nickel to quarter sized hail fell.
The hail was still in the gutters at sunrise.
Lots of dime to nickel sized hail fell along with very heavy rain.
Marble to quarter sized hail fell at Itasca State Park.
Lots of quarter sized hail fell along highway 89.
Very strong winds occurred with the large hail.
Large trees were blown down along the south side of Lake Bemidji.
Some siding was blown off of a building near the Pamida store south of Lake Bemidji.
Many trees were blown down and power poles snapped along Roosevelt Road and around northern Cass Lake.
There were reports of power poles snapped and power lines down in the Nymore area of southeast Bemidji and southeast Beltrami County.
Several streets south of downtown Bemidji had 1 to 2 feet of water flowing in them and at least one car was stranded.
The wind gust was measured at the Cooperstown airport.
Several large tree limbs were broken down in shelterbelts and area fields were impacted by the wind driven hail.
Pea to penny sized hail fell.

The roof of an open bay lumber storage building was uplifted and flipped eastward onto Junius Avenue. The section of roofing remained largely intact as it flipped and therefore it impacted and broke two adjacent power poles.
A large tree branch was blown down.
The hail was a mixture of nickel to quarter size.
The strong wind gusts occurred west of Hampden.
A shed was destroyed and two grain bins were blown off slab. Power poles were also blown down. Peak winds were estimated at 105 mph.
Several large tree branches and tree limbs were snapped off in shelterbelts along U. S. Highway 81.
Several large tree branches were broken down in shelterbelts along North Dakota highway 66.

Extensive damage occurred in Grafton. More than 50 large trees were blown down, including some 60 to 70 foot tall evergreens. Five houses and multiple vehicles were damaged by falling trees. One trailer house had substantial damage from a tree falling on it. The elevator in town was damaged, commercial buildings had metal siding blown off, and five or six utility poles were blown down. Several speed limit signs were bent over. Peak winds were estimated at 90 mph.
Several large tree branches and tree limbs were snapped off in shelterbelts along U. S. Highway 81.
Several large cottonwood trees and evergreens were snapped or uprooted in a farmyard. A metal flag pole was bent and shingles were tossed about.

Peak westerly winds to 121 mph were measured at the RWIS site located along highway 11. Damage to downwind fields, farm shelterbelts and the community of Donaldson were commensurate with winds to that extreme.

Two large commercial grade steel bins and their horizontal transfer system were torn out from the city grain elevator facility and were splayed to the east, partially blocking U. S. Highway 75. Several wooden power poles in the area were also snapped. Numerous large trees and tree limbs were torn down around the community and most homes sustained shingle, roofing and siding damage.

Three farm grade steel grain bins were torn off their foundations and blown out into a field. Three more steel bins at the farm yard were severely dented in and partially removed from their foundations. Numerous shingles were torn off of a home and all west facing windows on the home were cracked. A nearby metal highway signpost was snapped. Peak winds were estimated at 110 mph.

Several large tree branches were broken down in shelterbelts along U. S. Highway 75. Intermittent tree damage continued into and north of Stephen, from northern Tamarac Township into Sinnott Township.

Numerous large tree branches were broken down and several large trees, both oak and poplar, were snapped off in shelterbelts and groves near highway 11 through portions of both Springbrook and Deerwood townships.
Numerous large tree branches were broken down and several large trees, both oak and poplar, were snapped off in shelterbelts and groves across portions of central Nelson Park and Lincoln townships.
Numerous large tree branches were broken down and several large trees, both oak and poplar, were snapped off in shelterbelts and groves across portions of Arveson Township.
The peak wind was measured at the NDAWN mesonet site west of Greenbush on county road 4.
Numerous large tree branches were broken down and several large trees, both oak and poplar, were snapped off in shelterbelts and groves across portions of Deer and Lind townships.
Large tree branches were blown down.
Numerous nickel to quarter sized hail fell during very heavy rains and strong winds.

This tornado tracked eastward for about two miles and appears to have lifted just before reaching the Red River. The tornado was likely wrapped in downburst winds and rain as it tracked across the north side of Pembina. Though wind and hail occurred over a broad area of Pembina and Pembina East townships, there was more extreme tree branch damage and evidence of a tornado track across the north side of town. Peak winds were estimated at 85 mph.

This tornado touched down briefly in a farmyard and tracked southward for about one-half mile before lifting. The tornado tore off part of the house eaves and numerous shingles. It also spread sections of a ground based solar collector around the farmyard. Only small branches were broken down in the poplar trees to the northeast of the farmyard. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph.
One eight inch diameter tree and numerous tree limbs were snapped in a shelterbelt.

This tornado tracked for about two miles to the east-southeast and lifted about three miles northwest of Humboldt. The tornado broke down numerous large tree limbs in shelterbelts. Peak winds were estimated at 85 mph.  Wind and wind driven hail contributed to crop damages across central St. Vincent township.
The wind gust was measured by a NDSU NDAWN mesonet sensor.
The wind gust was measured by a NDSU NDAWN mesonet sensor.
The wind gust was measured by a MNDOT RWIS sensor along highway 89.

This weak tornado tracked for about a mile to around two miles southwest of Gentilly. Several large tree limbs were torn down, three trees were partially uprooted at a farmstead, and a few large tree limbs were torn down in a shelterbelt. Damage indicated peak winds of about 80 mph.
Several large tree branches and tree limbs were broken down by the winds. Some shingles were also blown off a house.

This tornado tracked for about 1.5 miles to around four miles east-northeast of Shelly. A couple of mature trees were snapped off and numerous smaller branches were spread around in a farmyard. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
The wind gust was measured by a NDSU NDAWN mesonet sensor.
The hail was described as being the size and shape of pears. Wind and wind driven hail completely flattened nearby crops in elkton township.
A couple of trees fell onto a camper trailer in the city park.
A few large tree branches and tree limbs were broken down around town.

A tornado was briefly viewed wrapped in heavy rains as it approached the northeast corner of Valley City. The tornado became entirely wrapped in heavy rains and downburst winds as it tracked for about three miles across northern portions of Valley City. Numerous large tree limbs and branches were broken down around town. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph. The downburst winds affected a much wider path.
Several three to five inch diameter tree branches were broken down in a shelterbelt.
An observer measured 2.80 inches of rain over the past 24 hours.

This tornado touched down in a farmstead shelterbelt just east of Lake Breckenridge and tracked near a second residence during its roughly one mile path. Some large trees were knocked down, a number of large branches were broken down and a few shingles were lifted off the house. A two cubic yard metal dumpster was lifted and thrown about 100 feet into a nearby ditch. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph.
The large hail fell over Devils Lake from Black Tiger Bay into East Bay.
Several sections of roadway and farm access roads were made impassable by water flowing across.
Several sections of county and farm access roads across southern Illinois and Dodds townships were made impassable due to water flowing over the roads.
An observer reported 3.50 inches of rain in Drayton. Water rose up to some car doors in town.
A brief touchdown with dust swirl was noted in a open field. Peak winds were estimated at 70 mph.
Two brief funnels were noted west and southwest from highway 32 along the Roseau and Marshall county line.
Street flooding was reported in Strathcona. Several farm access roads were also flooded near town.
Strong winds broke down a few large 3 to 5 inch diameter tree branches at a farmstead.
Numerous quarter to ping pong ball sized hail fell along with very heavy rain.

This tornado was briefly viewed by spotters near Goodridge. A 10 inch diameter ash tree was snapped about four feet above the ground. Several sections of tin roofing were torn off of a house and numerous large tree branches were blown down in shelterbelts and groves. Peak winds were estimated at 90 mph.
A brief touchdown in a open field was noted. Peak winds were estimated at 70 mph.
A persistent funnel cloud passed just east of the community of Thief River Falls during the Pennington County Fair.

Very strong wind and wind driven hail completely stripped fields of their crops for about a one mile wide by six mile long path through northeast King and northwest Brandsvold townships. Numerous large tree limbs were torn down for an additional half mile wide on either side of the main damage corridor. At one farmstead, a chicken coop was overturned and roofing materials were ripped loose from the house and barn.
A few large 3 to 5 inch diameter branches were broken down at a farmstead.
A few large trees were blown down at a farmstead. Wind damage continued intermittently through Tenney to Nashua, and across southern Campbell and Champion townships.
A few large tree branches and tree limbs were broken down in farmsteads and shelterbelts across Lawrence and North Ottawa townships.
A few large tree branches and tree limbs were broken down in a shelterbelt about one mile west of Squier.  Intermittent wind damage was evident across southern Aastad and Western townships.
A brief funnel was noted along the Canadian border, just to the east of the border crossing station. No touchdown was detected.
A few three to five inch diameter tree branches were broken down around town.
Numerous large tree branches were broken down in shelterbelts in southern Erdahl Township.
A few dime to quarter sized hail fell at the border crossing station.
A brief funnel cloud was observed south of Elliott, before it became obscured by rain.

Peak winds of 121 to 127 mph were measured at a temporary wind energy tower site. A total of six sensors arrayed from 130 to 200 feet above ground level registered the peak winds and rapid turning of winds from southeast, through west to northwest. This was consistent with a downburst wind at that site as depicted on radar, along with a bookend vortex and developing tornado located just north of the site.
A few large tree branches were broken down around town.

This tornado was enshrouded in downburst winds and heavy rains, but was briefly visible to spotters near Cogswell. The tornado ripped out nearly seven miles of dual wooden high voltage power line along its track. Numerous trees and singular power poles were snapped and pole sheds and steel grain bins were destroyed at multiple locations. Peak winds were estimated at 120 mph.

Numerous tree limbs were broken down around town. Fields were flattened by wind or stripped bare by wind driven hail. Wind damage occurred throughout Rutland and Dunbar townships from the 80 mph gusts.

This tornado was likely wrapped in heavy rains and downburst winds for much of its track. The tornado snapped or uprooted numerous elm and ash trees in farm shelterbelts and in the town of Delamere. Peak winds were estimated at 100 mph.

Numerous large tree limbs were broken down around town. Roofing materials were also torn off of buildings. Wind damage throughout Ransom and Kingston townships indicated widespread peak winds from 70 to 80 mph with episodes of wind driven hail.
Numerous large tree limbs were broken down in shelterbelts across southern Rosemeade Township.
The tornado became enshrouded in heavy rains and downburst winds. Several trees were snapped or uprooted in farm shelterbelts. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph.
Numerous large tree limbs were broken down and some shingles were torn off homes in Mooreton. Widespread wind damage was evident throughout Barney and Mooreton townships.
Trees were blown down at a farmstead, including a tree leaning on a house. The surrounding shelterbelts did not have as much damage.
Numerous large tree branches were broken down in Fairmount and in neighboring sections of Fairmount Township.

The tornado touchdown was visible from near Ayr. Tree branches and limbs were broken down along a narrow path in two shelterbelts. Two smaller trees were snapped and thrown about in a farm yard. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
A few nickel to quarter sized hail fell along with brief heavy rains and strong winds.

Two to three inches of rain fell within an hour causing local street flooding. Several sections of farmland and farm access roads near the confluence of the Wild Rice River (ND) and the Red River were also inundated as these local rivers were already above local flood stage.
The wind gust was measured by a MNDOT RWIS sensor near Dilworth.
Several large tree branches and limbs were broken down around Hawley.
Several sections of rural road in Dunn Township were flooded.

Heavy rainfall of two to five inches on top of previously saturated soils produced extensive runoff into the Redeye River drainage. Localized flooding occurred near the river in eastern Evergreen and western Spruce Grove townships.

Heavy rainfall of two to five inches on top of previously saturated soils produced excessive runoff into the Redeye River drainage. Localized flooding occurred near the river through portions of Butler and Paddock townships.

Heavy rainfall of two to five inches on top of previously saturated soils produced excessive runoff into the Redeye River drainage. Localized flooding occurred near the river through portions of Redeye and Rockwood townships.
A few large three to five inch diameter tree branches and tree limbs were broken down by strong winds at a campground.
Two trees were snapped in a shelterbelt east of Interstate 29 near mile post 114. A ND DOT RWIS sensor located two miles to the southwest measured peak winds of 55 mph.
Flooding occurred along a farm access road and several sections of farmland in eastern Osage and western Hamlin townships. Ditches flowing into Silver Creek overflowed.
A tree was snapped in a shelterbelt along Interstate 29.
A tree was snapped and a wooden roadside sign was broken down.
Five to ten inch diameter tree branches were blown down.
A few large branches were blown down.
Several large three to five inch diameter tree branches were broken down at a farmstead. Power lines were also blown down.
Corn fields were flattened by winds.
Several trees were uprooted and large tree branches were snapped off in farm yards and shelterbelts in central Higdem Township.
A few trees were snapped in a shelterbelt south of highway 11.
Numerous trees were snapped or uprooted in shelterbelts across much of Springbrook Township.
A few large tree branches and limbs were broken down.
Three wooden power poles were snapped along highway 59. Numerous nearby poplar trees were also snapped.
Several large cottonwood, poplar and boxelder trees were snapped or uprooted in a farm yard. Shingles were also torn off of roofs and flying tree branches were embedded in roofs.
The roof was ripped off of a 180 foot long hay shed. Numerous tree limbs were broken down in farmsteads across Nereson Township.
Several large tree limbs were broken down around Oak Island.
A large number of trees were severely damaged across northern Laona Township. Mature pine trees were snapped off midway up.
Widespread wind damage was noted across Deerwood and Arveson townships. Numerous large tree limbs were broken down in yards, shelterbelts, and groves. Peak winds were estimated at 85 to 95 mph.
A cold core funnel dropped out of the clouds near downtown Grand Forks.

Peak 3 second wind gusts of from 128 to 145 mph were measured by 6 different wind sensors placed at heights of from 160 to 380 feet AGL at a temporary wind energy monitoring tower site.  Peak 3 second wind gusts of 119 mph were measured at a height of 20 feet AGL at this same tower site.  These measurements were made as a tornado struck the site, and just prior to the collapse of the tower.

A several acre area of burning grassland and slough produced a pyrocumulus cloud and brief fire whirls.  One of the fire whirls and its associated rotating updraft plume  briefly extended as a contiguous vortex from near the surface to the cloud base, constituting a very weak and non-damaging fire tornado.  the fire whirl was located about 5 miles north of the community of Loma.
Parts of county road 3 were under water from the heavy rain and flash flooding.
Reports of 4.00 to 6.50 inches of rain were received from Hankinson. This filled ditches and quickly covered some roads and streets in town.
Heavy rain quickly filled ditches and covered several rural roads.
An empty seed bin was tossed off its foundation into a grain conveyor, bending the conveyor.
Pea to dime sized hail fell about one inch deep on the highway.

This tornado touched down near a farmstead west of Minnesota highway 9 and tracked eastward for about one quarter of mile before lifting. A spotter reported several four foot by six foot tin roofing panels were blown off a pole shed and carried eastward across Minnesota highway 9. Peak winds were estimated at 70 to 80 mph.

This tornado touched down near a farmstead and then tracked intermittently to the east for about a half mile. The tornado tore all of the tin roofing and roof panels from an open faced pole shed. It also tore down several tree limbs in the farmyard and tossed a trampoline on top of the garage. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.

This tornado touched down near a farmstead and tracked eastward for about two miles before lifting. The tornado popped three empty steel grain bins off their concrete pads and tumbled them around quite violently. The tornado also tore the doors off an enclosed pole shed, tore the roofing panels off, and uplifted and displaced the rafters. Two young men working at the farmstead witnessed the tornado approaching and sought shelter in the damaged pole shed but were not injured. Peak winds were estimated at 90 mph.

Multiple funnels were observed across central Clay County from near Felton towards Ulen and down through the Dilworth and Glyndon areas toward Downer. These occurred mainly from 1123 to 1200 CST. Most were short lived but one or more were persistent for several minutes.
Multiple brief funnels were observed moving eastward across Wilkin County. One of these produced a very brief and non-damaging ground contact near the intersection of county roads 16 and 19.
In inch or more of pea to penny sized hail caused very icy conditions along stretches of Interstate 94 in northeastern Grant County.
Pea to nickel sized hail completely covered the ground.
Trees were uprooted in Cayuga from the strong winds.
Trees were uprooted near Mantador due to the strong winds.
The wind gust was measured by the Gwinner, North Dakota AWOS. Several power poles were snapped along a section line near Gwinner.

The 2315 CST observation from the Wahpeton airport AWOS came in with a gust to 65 knots. The time was estimated by radar. The 83 mph wind gust was measured by a personal weather station located just south of the airport. A private hanger door was caved in by the wind which caused some damage to an airplane parked just inside the door.
The hail varied in size from mothball to quarter size.
In the Weetown area north of Fergus Falls, boats were blown onto roads, fish houses were tipped over, and trailers and trees were blown over.
About one-half mile of power poles were snapped near the intersection of county roads 16 and 1. A barn and silo at a farmstead were heavily damaged. Peak winds were estimated at 80 to 90 mph.

Damaging thunderstorm winds tracked from the Fish Lake area into the West Long Lake area to near Phelps Mill. Several poplar trees were snapped, some shingles and house trim was torn loose, and one loosely anchored shed was thrown across the road and destroyed. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
Pea to nickel sized hail completely blanketed the fields.
Numerous dime to quarter sized hail nearly covered the ground.
Very heavy rain and lots of dime to quarter sized hail fell.

The storm left banks of mainly dime to nickel sized hail covering the ground, although there were also some quarter sized hail in the mix. Heavy rain and moderate to strong winds accompanied the hail.
Nickel to quarter sized hail fell with gusty winds. Some garden damage was reported.
Small trees were blown down at a residence near the intersection of U. S. Highway 2 and county road 45, near Grace Lake.
A 100 yard row of trees were flattened from south to north. The area impacted was along Roosevelt Road just west of School Lake.
Quarter size hail fell along with some smaller hailstones.
Several ash and oak trees up to 22 inches in diameter were snapped at the Turtle River State Park.
Several trees were blown down in Larimore.
The wind gust was measured at the Grand Forks Air Force Base.
Numerous three to four inch diameter tree limbs were blown down in a yard.
Nickel sized hail fell at the intersection of highways 55 and 75.

A tornado touched down along Interstate 29 near the south Drayton exit. The tornado tracked intermittently to the southeast before crossing the Red River. Tree limbs were snapped and branches were scattered in at least three sets of shelterbelts along the route. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph. This tornado continued into northwest Marshall County in Minnesota.
Very strong winds were also reported which blew down some tree branches in the yard.
Pea to penny sized hail fell along with very strong winds.

This long, thin, and rope like tornado lasted for just a couple of minutes. It tracked eastward for about one mile, nearly to the Avon and Pleasant View township line. Numerous large branches were knocked down in a farmstead shelterbelt and a couple of large tree limbs were snapped off in a field shelterbelt. Peak winds were estimated at 70 mph.

This rope like tornado lasted for over four minutes and tracked due east for nearly two miles in the far northwest corner of Union Township. Several tree tops were snapped in field shelterbelts and at least one tree was uprooted near a farm shelterbelt. Peak winds were estimated at 90 mph.
Approximately the top thirty feet of a 100 foot tall cottonwood tree was twisted off as a gust front pushed through a farmstead.

After the storms went through the Petersburg area a thin funnel cloud appeared on the back edge of the cloud line. It appeared to be just south of Petersburg but was more distant and more closely viewed over east central Alder Township. From a distance the funnel appeared to be near the ground but as viewed from nearby the funnel remained several hundred feet above the tree tops.

A persistent funnel was viewed from exit 168 on Interstate 29. Intermittent tornado touchdowns occurred along a three mile path, which resulted in tree limbs being snapped in several shelterbelts along the route. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.

This tornado appeared to have started as a ground based dust devil which grew vertically into a landspout but dissipated fairly quickly. The path occurred over open fields and peak winds were estimated at 65 mph.

This tornado originated in Walsh County, North Dakota, at 1707 CST. The tornado tracked intermittently for about three miles in Marshall County, where it snapped tree limbs and branches in several shelterbelts along its track. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.

This tornado snapped several trees and tree limbs while scattering branches from at least three shelterbelts along its path. Shingles were torn from farm buildings. Peak winds were estimated at 90 mph.
This funnel was partially rain wrapped.
Very strong winds accompanied the hail and tore a few shingles off the roof of a house.

A persistent funnel was seen approaching the Norcross area from eastern Traverse County for several minutes before it crossed into western Grant County.

A weak tornado touched down just west of highway 9 and tracked intermittently eastward for about three miles. The tornado broke down several large tree branches and a few tree limbs in shelterbelts along its path. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
Strong winds blew down fifty foot tall pine trees.
This funnel cloud briefly reached about one-third to one-half way down to the ground.

This tornado snapped several cottonwood and ash trees in farm shelterbelts and two wooden power poles along a county road. Stacked and banded steel roofing panels were scattered in one farm yard and a metal dumpster was thrown about fifty yards. The peak winds were estimated at 100 mph.

Crops were flattened in the Sarles area and objects were blown over at a construction site.

Three steel grain bins were caved in and blown off their foundations. Many trees were blown down and several windows were broken or blown out of homes.
A twenty-four inch diameter tree was blown down along with several power lines. Pea size hail was also reported along with six to eight inches of water on main street.
Trees were blown down in Hensel. A local farmer lost a pole barn and garage and some farm equipment was damaged.
A tree branch almost four feet in circumference was blown down.
Sixty to seventy mph wind gusts were reported but no damage occurred.
A few trees were knocked down by the strong wind.

Lightning caused a house fire that led to a total structural loss.

Heavy rains in excess of four inches in two hours across much of Advance and Cavalier North townships produced significant runoff in local creeks that feed into the Tongue River. One small creek washed out a box culvert/bridge along 98th Street Northeast, between 138th and 139th Avenue Northeast.

Mostly pea size hail fell, but there were a few stones the size of nickels and quarters.
Intermittent large hail fell with very heavy rain.
Heavy rains overwhelmed the city lift station and produced widespread street flooding through the early morning. Some water got into structures like garages and outbuildings.
Several large tree branches were also blown down.
The spotter also reported 1.36 inches of rain.
Dime to half dollar size hail fell near the Shooting Star Casino.
Several trees were blown down in shelterbelts near Interstate 29 between mile points 52 and 54.
The peak wind was measured at a NDAWN mesonet site.
Golf ball to hen egg sized hail fell.

At least one large tree and several large tree branches were blown down in Grafton.
A large cottonwood tree was blown over.
A few large trees and several large tree branches were blown down or snapped by the wind in and near Drayton.
Numerous three to six inch diameter tree branches were blown down. Power outages were also reported in the Hillsboro area.
A few trees and several large branches were blown down in various shelterbelts in northern Deerhorn Township.
A large tree was blown down across county road 7.

The tornado touched down about a mile west of the airport and tracked to the Interstate 94 exit north of town by 2230 CST. The tornado continued to about four miles northeast of town, a track length of about seven miles. The tornado was likely wrapped in heavy rain during portions of this track. One livestock loafing shed was lifted and collapsed and several trees were knocked down. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
A funnel cloud was observed between Kent and Wolverton.
The peak wind was measured by the AWOS at the Hallock airport. Several structures were damaged at the North Star Industries facility located south of the airport.
At least one large oak tree and several large tree branches were blown down in and near Hallock.
Four inch diameter tree branches were blown down near Clay County Road 10 between Donner and Rollag.
Several trees were blown down, blocking a township road in rural St. Joseph Township.
A few trees were toppled in shelterbelts along U. S. Highway 75.
Several large trees and tree branches were blown down by the wind.

Several large trees and large tree branches were blown down across portions of Home Lake and Flom townships in southeast Norman County. East of Flom falling trees damaged a barn roof and several smaller sheds.
Numerous large trees were blown down near Waubun and in rural areas of Poplar Grove and Lake Grove townships.
Several large trees and large tree branches were broken down in Naytahwaush and across northern portions of the White Earth State Forest.
A few four to six inch diameter tree branches were broken down around the park. Very strong winds blew for several minutes.

Three to four inches of rain in three hours produced widespread street flooding, flooding of underpasses, storm sewer backup, and basement flooding across the Fargo area. Water was reported to be up to the bases of fire hydrants near 45th Street and 12th Avenue North, making the roads impassable. River levels in town were already above minor flood stage due to previous heavy rainfall in the area, which meant that storm sewer flap gates were closed and pumping stations were likely overwhelmed by the high local runoff rates.

The North Dakota Highway Patrol and North Dakota DOT personnel closed Interstate 94 at the Casselton exit due to water flowing across all four lanes. Traffic was detoured across the exit ramps until flood waters had subsided.
Farm yards and fields were flooded near Christine.
Widespread flooding was reported in and around Wolverton. A total of 8.25 inches of rain was reported in town with over nine inches reported just outside of town to the south.
Water was reported over U. S. Highway 75 near Kent.

Overland flooding developed over portions of Holy Cross Township drained by Wolverton Creek. Four to eight inches of rainfall during the preceding evening collected in farm fields, ditches, and smaller streams through the early morning then steadily drained towards Wolverton Creek and the Red River. Wolverton Creek overtopped and partially washed out rural and township roads at several locations.

Overland flooding developed over portions of Wolverton Township drained by Wolverton Creek. Six to ten inches of very heavy rainfall the preceding evening collected in farm fields, ditches, and smaller streams through the early morning then steadily drained towards Wolverton Creek and the Red River. Wolverton Creek overtopped and partially washed out rural township and county roads at several locations.

Overland flooding developed over portions of rural Eagle Township. Four to eight inches of very heavy rainfall from the preceding evening collected in farm fields, ditches, and small streams through the early morning then steadily drained towards the Red River during the day. County and township roads were overtopped and partially washed out at several locations.

A pronounced landspout type funnel developed north of Detroit Lakes from a southward moving cumuliform cloud. A cell phone video clip provided by a traveler on U. S. Highway 10 north of downtown Detroit Lakes showed the weak funnel extending to within a few hundred feet of the ground and persisting for almost a minute.
Several six inch diameter branches were blown down near Leeds.
Several six inch diameter tree branches were blown down near Cando.
Dime to quarter sized hail and very strong winds occurred in central Springfield Township.

Damaging winds took down power lines near Wyndmere, leading to a loss of power to observation equipment at the Wyndmere airport. Power lines were repaired and power was restored later that morning.
Widespread street and basement flooding occurred in Gwinner. The Bobcat plant was partially flooded with several inches of water on the floor.
Highway 13 was closed west of Gwinner due to water washing over the road.
North Dakota Highway 32 was closed between Gwinner and Lisbon at Dead Colt Creek.
A pickup was swept off North Dakota Highway 32 into Dead Colt Creek. The vehicle floated downstream and was eventually submerged resulting in one fatality by 8 am CDT.
Heavy rains and flash flooding caused temporary road closures along North Dakota Highway 18 near Wyndmere.
The hail fell with very heavy rain.
The wind gust was measured at the Cooperstown airport.
Numerous large six to eight inch diameter tree branches were broken down in shelterbelts across northern Broadlawn and Galesburg townships.
Lots of quarter size hail fell along highway 200A in the Blanchard area, covering roads an inch or two deep and making the ditches white.
A storm chaser observed a small rope tornado.

Dime to quarter sized hail covered the sides of Interstate 29 north of Grandin.
Dime to quarter sized hail fell near Grandin.
Quarter to ping pong ball sized hail fell at the campground along with very heavy rain and strong winds.

The hail fell with winds of 50 to 60 mph.
Large tree branches were blown down near Interstate 94.
Dime to quarter size hail fell.
The hail was accompanied by 45 to 50 mph winds.
A tree was blown down at a farmstead along with many smaller branches.
Nickel sized hail and very heavy rain was also reported.
A semi truck and trailer were blown over along Interstate 29 near mile post 76.
A large tree was blown down, blocking the road at 10th Street South and 13th Avenue.
Large tree branches were blown down.
Half dollar sized hail fell along with winds in excess of 70 mph.
Due to electrical outages, pump failure, and water pooling at the Interstate 94 exit near Casselton, the North Dakota DOT temporarily closed both lanes and detoured traffic over the exit ramps.
The hail fell with very strong winds.

The observer at Baldhill Dam measured 3.10 inches of rain in a short amount of time. Roads near the dam were quickly covered with water and debris. Farmyards and fields in the area also experienced localized flooding.

Very heavy rains produced widespread street flooding around Valley City. Power outages and rapid runoff also combined to produce flooding of storm drains and sewer backup issues. At least four homes had partially collapsed basement walls. About 6.30 inches of rain fell over a two to three hour period.
Golf ball to hen egg to tennis ball sized hail fell.
Quarter sized hail and strong winds were reported along the north side of Big Cormorant Lake.
A few six to eight inch diameter tree limbs were blown down. At least one garage roof was also damaged as a result.
Many large tree branches were blown down and a few trees were toppled by the strong winds. Some small hail also fell along with over three inches of rain.
Numerous boats, boat lifts, and docks were blown onshore due to strong winds and wave action on Battle Lake.
Dime to quarter sized hail fell.
Pea to quarter sized hail fell at the Molls Berry Farm.
Strong thunderstorm winds caused widespread damage to boat docks, boat lifts, boats, and trees around Otter Tail Lake.

Strong winds and large hail affected the southeast corner of Toad Lake Township. Winds lofted an open faced loafing shed and pulled several of the support posts out of the ground. Numerous large tree branches and limbs were broken down in farm yards resulting in some roof damage.
Three to five inch diameter tree branches were felled.
Several large trees and power lines were blown down. Many three to six inch diameter tree branches were also broken off in town.
The wind gust was measured by a MNDOT RWIS sensor along highway 10.
The wind gust was estimated by a trained spotter.
The wind was measured by a MNDOT RWIS sensor along Interstate 94.
A period of high winds followed behind earlier thunderstorm activity from west central into central Minnesota. A few trees were toppled or large branches broken down across portions of Wadena County.

Runoff from heavy rains caused widespread flooding of local ditches, creeks, and fields across Corliss and Butler townships. County road eight east of county road 53 was closed for about half a day due to washouts along the shoulder. The city of Perham also experienced areas of street flooding.
A 5,000 bushel steel grain bin was blown down by the strong winds.
Quarter size hail fell along U. S. Highway 2 on the north side of Grand Forks.
The hail fell at 55th street and 8th avenue north.
The heavy rain cause minor street flooding in Lidgerwood.
A wall cloud was also observed to the south.
A brief tornado touchdown was viewed over open rangeland. A dust plume was raised but no damage was otherwise observed. Peak winds were estimated at 70 mph.
Heavy rainfall was also reported.
Numerous three to five inch diameter tree branches were broken down around the area. There was also quite a bit of dime to nickel size hail.
Several dead trees were blown down over a road. Very heavy rainfall was also reported.
A large cottonwood tree was blown over between Nashua and Tintah.
Several six to eight inch diameter tree branches were blown down in Elbow Lake.
Light poles, power lines, and hundreds of trees were blown down. Peak winds across the central part of town were estimated at 60 to 80 mph.

Significant wind damage occurred on the southeast side of Thief River Falls. Numerous roofs were damaged, a motor home was flipped, and billboards were bent or broken. Several trailer homes were damaged and one was flipped. Several garages had roofs removed or were collapsed. Peak winds were estimated at 95 to 105 mph and occurred for a couple of minutes.
Numerous large hardwood trees were uprooted or had trunks snapped along the banks of the Red Lake River. Peak winds were estimated at 100 to 110 mph.

Extreme winds snapped a dozen wooden power poles, uprooted numerous trees and caved in or otherwise demolished several large capacity steel grain bins and other outbuildings at a farm site. The tree damage extended across much of southern Silverton and northern Smiley townships. Peak winds were estimated at 110 to 120 mph.
Several large tree branches and limbs were blown down in shelterbelts across southern Clover Leaf and northern Kratka townships. A nearby NDAWN wind sensor measured peak winds of 55 mph.
A few three to five inch diameter tree branches were blown down along the southern edge of Cando.
A few three to five inch diameter tree branches were blown down in a farm shelterbelt along with some pea to penny sized hail and brief heavy rain.
Three inch diameter branches were blown down.
The tornado snapped about six wooden power poles along county road 17 before it dissipated. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph.
Strong winds blew down small branches and uprooted one tree. Hail damage to crops was also reported.
The strong wind blew over several trees.
Hail fell in sizes up to golf ball size.
Several 1,600 pound round hay bales were tossed or tumbled across a field in northern Como township.

This tornado continued into Clearwater County before it dissipated. The tornado snapped and uprooted numerous trees along its path. Peak winds were estimated at 90 mph. The entire path length across the two counties was nearly 7 miles.

This tornado began in Polk County, about one mile north of Trail, at 12:33 am CST. The tornado snapped and uprooted numerous trees along its entire seven mile path. Peak winds were estimated at 90 mph.

This tornado continued into Clearwater County, where it lifted at about 0130 am CST, west-northwest of Zerkel. The tornado damaged structures at three locations along the route with long tracks of tree and crop damage evident. Peak winds were estimated at 115 mph.

This tornado began in Mahnomen County, just southeast of Mahnomen, at 12:50 am CST. The total tornado track was about 21 miles. The tornado damaged structures at three locations along the route with long tracks of tree and crop damage. Peak winds were estimated at 115 mph.

A downburst wind damage path developed across west central Greenwood Township. Numerous trees were toppled with some falling on the Greenwood Township Hall roof. A one to two mile wide swath of wind damage extended for over three miles and indicated peak winds of 60 to 80 mph.

A microburst damage area was produced across the northeast quarter of section 30 in Rapid River Township. The downburst initiated across the southwest corner of a farmstead and projected to the east and northeast across the farmyard. A steel pole shed was torn open and demolished with debris impacted and denting several steel grain bins along the east end of the yard. Several pine trees and two power poles in the yard were snapped by the wind. Peak winds were estimated at 95 to 105 mph.
Many trees were damaged and tin roof panels were peeled off of a shed.
A fair amount of penny sized hail fell and drifted, causing some minor garden damage.
Penny to quarter sized hail covered highway 59.

Winds blew down two large oak trees and seven cottonwood trees, which blocked a road. There was a significant amount of quarter to half inch hail, sufficient to drift and remain on the ground until evening.
Shingles were blown off a roof and numerous trees were blown down. A significant amount of quarter to half inch hail covered the ground for a period of time after the storm passed.
Several three to five inch diameter tree branches were broken down near Sandy Lake.
Several poplar trees were pushed over or snapped by the strong wind.
Strong winds also blew open the garage doors.
A few three to five inch diameter tree branches were broken down. Pea to penny sized hail also fell.
Quarter to half dollar sized hail fell near Litchville.
Large hail cracked the windshield on a vehicle.

A few pea to penny sized hail fell.
A large wind driven hail swath developed across southern Colfax-West Township and northern Nansen Township. In several sections of farmland crops were shattered down to stems and stumps.
Hail covered Interstate 29 near exit 31.
Several minutes of dime to quarter sized hail fell along with very strong winds.

A swath of large hail and damaging winds to 70 mph produced widespread tree and crop damage across central Dwight-West Township. In the town of Dwight, a few large trees were snapped at the base while large tree branches were broken off throughout the town.
A persistent wall cloud with a brief funnel was viewed from northwest Wahpeton.

A brief tornado touchdown occurred near a farmstead and broke numerous large tree branches and limbs which then damaged an occupied tractor cab and nearby farm outbuildings. This tornado appeared to become quickly engulfed in driving rain and hail. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.

A partially rain and hail wrapped tornado tracked intermittently for about three miles. The tornado snapped several trees in a series of shelterbelts and threw large tree limbs well into the fields. Peak winds were estimated at 90 mph. The tornado likely crossed Interstate 29 near mile point 29 during this period.
Hail up to hen egg size fell.

Wind driven hail produced widespread tree damage across northern and eastern neighborhoods in Wahpeton. Numerous large trees or tree limbs were snapped off near ground level while neighborhoods were littered with smaller branches, leaf debris, and hail. Peak winds were estimated at 75 mph with the strong winds lasting for several minutes.
A few large hailstones fell along with very strong winds and driving rain.
Half dollar sized hail fell.
Several three to five inch diameter tree branches were broken down in farm shelterbelts after a short burst of strong winds and very heavy rain. Some pea sized hail also fell.

Numerous large trees were blown down. Power poles and power lines were blown down. An entire steel roof was torn off its rafters and flung southeastward across Minnesota Avenue. Impacts from the debris broke down a steel street light pole and caused incidental damage to other buildings across the street. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
Strong winds and very heavy rainfall was also reported.
Hail up to 1.5 inches in diameter also fell with the very strong winds. Numerous large tree branches were also blown down.
Nickel to quarter sized hail fell with swirling winds.
The tops of a few cottonwood trees were broken off.

The wind gust was measured at the MNDOT RWIS site located along Interstate 94 outside of Rothsay. The local power company reported that localized power outages began around this time across northeast Wilkin County and northwest Otter Tail County, due to broken tree limbs falling across power lines.

Flooding occurred along the Middle River in the town of Middle River, causing a few streets to be closed and several spots to be sandbagged. Farm fields and farm access roads were also flooded near the Middle River in eastern Spruce Valley and western Cedar townships.

Heavy rain led to street, basement, and trailer park flooding near Wadena. A total of eight inches of rain was measured in Wadena.

The top four feet of two forty foot evergreen trees were broken off and an older tree was blown down.

Campers at the Mount Carmel Recreation Area Campground reported a funnel cloud within the lightning, but could not tell if it reached the ground.

Softball sized holes in a lawn were made by large hail that fell north-northeast of Langdon. Windshields were busted out and there was major damage to the siding on a house. Major crop damage was also reported.
Tennis ball to baseball sized hail fell across portions of northern Westhope and northwest Hope townships.

Several trees were blown down around town. One eight inch diameter tree fell on a deck, which resulted in some damage to the fencing. An automobile with attached trailer were moved and the trailer was twisted and collapsed.

Three large 50,000 bushel steel grain bins were partially caved in at a farmstead and numerous large tree branches and limbs were broken off across central Pleasant Prairie Township.

Numerous large tree branches and limbs were broken down across Columbia and western Cherry Lake townships. At two nearby farmsteads, one steel clad pole shed was collapsed, several steel grain bins were caved in, roofing was blown off a cattle shed, and other farm outbuildings were damaged. At another farmstead, one garage was blown down and several trees were snapped or uprooted.

A funnel formed northwest of McHenry (which is actually located in Foster County), north of the Eddy/Foster county line, and touched down near highway 20. The tornado then tracked intermittently to the east-northeast for about eight miles (about four miles of this occurred in Eddy County), to around three miles west-northwest of Red Willow Lake (in Griggs County). Numerous large tree tree branches were broken down or tree trunks snapped along the damage path. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.

This tornado began in Eddy County at 1835 CST, with its first four miles of track in that county. The tornado crossed into Griggs County at 1841 CST and tracked intermittently to the east-northeast for about another four miles (the total track was about eight miles), where it ended about three miles west-northwest of Red Willow Lake. Numerous large tree branches were broken down or tree trunks snapped along the path. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
A brief touchdown was observed over open country near the Sheyenne River. Peak winds were estimated at 70 mph.
There were also numerous tree branches broken down.
Portions of tin roofing were blown off of a county building.
Several large diameter trees were snapped near the golf course.

Widespread tree damage occurred throughout Newburgh and Garfield townships in northeast Steele County. At one homestead north of Hatton, several poplar trees were snapped and a patio cover was torn off a house and demolished. Tree damage continued into adjacent townships in Grand Forks and Traill counties.

This tornado tracked intermittently for about eight miles before ending about two miles south-southeast of Arvilla. The tornado snarled trees in shelterbelts and broke down numerous large tree branches, limbs, and whole tree trunks along its path. A few rural residences and farm buildings had shingles torn off, quonset doors ripped off, and outbuildings damaged. Peak winds were estimated at 90 mph.
Two trees, one 25 inches in diameter and the other 30 inches in diameter, were snapped in a yard. Power lines were also knocked down in Thompson.
Numerous large tree branches and limbs and several tree trunks were snapped off due to prolonged periods of damaging winds.
Widespread wind damaged was noted in shelterbelts across Union Township. Numerous large tree branches and limbs were broken down and an occasional tree trunk was snapped.
A funnel cloud was viewed from Turtle River State Park.
A few large trees were snapped along Gateway Drive. This was the third episode of damaging winds in that area for the evening.
Several large tree branches and limbs were broken down in shelterbelts across northern Abercrombie Township.

The tornado, which was wrapped in heavy rains and damaging downburst winds, tracked from near Eldred, through the south side of Crookston, through Gentilly, where it crossed into Red Lake County and ended about eight miles east-southeast of Red Lake Falls. The tornado snapped or uprooted numerous trees along its path, tore sections of roofing off of buildings and residences, tumbled empty rail cars, and snapped power poles along its nearly 38 mile path (about 25 miles in Polk County). Peak winds were estimated at 120 mph.

This tornado began near Eldred, in Polk County, at 1952 CST. From Eldred, it tracked across the south side of Crookston, through Gentilly, where it crossed into Red Lake County about four miles east-northeast of Gentilly. From this point it continued east-northeast to a point about eight miles east-southeast of Red Lake Falls. The total track length was about 38 miles, with about 13 miles of the total in Red Lake County. The tornado was wrapped in heavy rains and damaging downburst winds and it snapped or uprooted numerous trees along its path, tore sections of roofing off of buildings and residences, tumbled empty rail cars, and snapped power poles. Peak winds were estimated at 120 mph.
The hail was accompanied by very heavy rain which led to ponding water.
A funnel cloud descended and then ascended from a rotating wall cloud.
A personal weather station recorded a wind gust of 80 mph. The strong winds wrecked havoc on the trees in the city of Crookston.

Nickel to half dollar sized hail cracked the windshield and lights on a fire truck. The hail covered the ground, making it appear white.
Numerous six to eight inch diameter tree branches were broken down from a farmyard eastward to the Red River.
Significant tree and property damage were reported.

This tornado snapped or uprooted numerous trees along its path. Several farm outbuildings, steel grain bins, and a steel pole shed were completely destroyed. One farmstead sized wooden grain elevator was completely dismantled and sections of it were thrown dozens of yards. Multiple power poles were snapped at different locations. Peak winds were estimated at 130 mph.
Quarter to half dollar sized hail fell.
Significant damage was reported to a barn, steel pole shed, and numerous trees at a farmstead about three miles east of Northcote.
Tennis ball sized hail fell after a tornado passed off to the east.
Numerous large tree branches and tree trunks were snapped across portions of southeast Percy Township.
Several four to six inch diameter tree branches were broken down in area shelterbelts.

The tornado snapped or uprooted numerous trees along its path, destroyed two steel grain bins at one farmstead, and severely damaged three more at subsequent farmsteads. Steel roofing panels and doors were town off of pole sheds and flung dozens of yards. Peak winds were estimated at 100 mph.
The peak wind was measured by the NDAWN mesonet station along county road 4. The winds were likely induced by the passing tornado.
It was estimated that the rotation was at least one mile across.
Wind driven hail broke several windows.
Ping pong ball sized hail lasted five minutes.

Numerous trees six inches in diameter and larger were broken down across northern Lake West and Lake East townships. One power pole was broken out by lightning and power lines were taken down at multiple locations.
Several ten to twenty foot tall pine trees were blown over during a protracted period of heavy rain and strong gusty winds.
An eight inch diameter cherry tree was split roughly four feet above the ground. One portion of the tree fell on the back of a car.
The strong wind gust was measured at the Grafton airport.
Three large jack pines were blown down across a fence. One of the trees also fell onto the roof of a house.

Tin roofing panels and attached pieces of board and insulation were torn from an old widespan poultry barn, with pieces of debris knocking down power lines and blowing onto highway80. The old barn was being used for storage.
Drifts of pea size hail were also reported.
Strong thunderstorm outflow produced a broad area of blowing dust and one or more brief gustnadoes along the outflow boundary.
Three to four inches of rain fell in a short duration, flooding ditches, fields, and farm access roads across portions of Westend and Homestead townships.
Three to four inches of rain fell in a short duration, flooding ditches, fields, and farm access roads across portions of eastern Sandoun Township.

The tornado tracked for about two miles across southern Acton Township. Several medium to large cottonwood trees twelve to eighteen inches in diameter were snapped near the ground and numerous tree branches and limbs were broken off in shelterbelts along the path. Peak winds were estimated at 85 mph.
The hail was accompanied by very heavy rain and strong winds. Several large branches and tree limbs were broken down in a farmyard.
The cooperative observer reported hail with very little rainfall.

A persistent wall cloud and funnel tracked from just east of Alvarado into far northwest Polk County. No touchdown or associated damage was observed.

Several trees were blown down and boats and docks were overturned on Duck Lake.

A one foot diameter tree was snapped at the base. It then fell on a nearby propane tank.
Several three to five inch diameter tree branches were broken off in a farmyard. A home weather station there measured 58 mph winds.

Pea to nickel sized hail fell.

A weak tornado kicked up dust on the ground. An observer indicated the circulation was on the ground for about three minutes. No property damage occurred as the tornado remained over open fields the entire time. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
A spotter located west of Cooperstown reported the end of the short track tornado as it lifted.

A fifty foot tall tree was blown down.

A tornado tracked across southern portions of the city of Mahnomen, where it ripped roofing off of a maintenance shed, lifted and tipped a parked semi trailer, slid parked vehicles, and destroyed a small wooden shed. Flying debris impacted and damaged additional vehicles and structures near the casino. Peak wind speeds were estimated at 95 mph.
Quarter to half dollar sized hail fell.
A rope tornado touched down in open fields east of Osnabrock. Peak wind speeds were estimated at 70 mph.
Nickel to quarter sized hail fell in the town of Concrete and at the nearby Cavalier Air Force Station.

The tornado touched down west of Milton and tracked into the southwestern side of town before dissipating. Eight empty grain cars in a grain train at the Milton loading facility were blown over to the southwest. Peak wind speeds were estimated at 90 mph.

The tornado tracked from two miles north-northwest of Union, through town, and to about one mile south of Union. The tornado snapped numerous cottonwood and oak trees along its path. It also snapped one power pole and twisted a road sign. Peak wind speeds were estimated at 100 mph.
This tornado tracked across mainly open fields, kicking up a red and black dirt plume. The tornado was viewed and photographed by numerous trained spotters. Peak wind speeds were estimated at 85 mph.

The tornado tracked across a shelterbelt and along the edge of a farmstead. A few large branches were broken down and tossed across the field, but no structures were hit. Peak wind speeds were estimated at 75 mph.
The tornado remained over open fields east of Fordville. Peak winds were estimated at 75 mph.
This funnel cloud was viewed from the Grand Forks International Airport.

The tornado touched down along the eastern edge of the Forest River Colony and passed just west of Inkster, before dissipating about two miles east-northeast of Orr. The tornado was observed by Grand Forks Air Force Base personnel at about 408 p. m. CST. A few oak trees were snapped in the Forest River Valley while other large tree branches were broken down in shelterbelts along its path. Peak winds were estimated at 100 mph.
The tornado was viewed in open country south of highway 15 moving east.
The tornado touchdown was brief and in an open field.
A tornado briefly touched down in an open field.

The remaining funnel cloud was visible for several more minutes after the tornado lifted. The tornado broke down large branches in shelterbelts along its path. Peak winds were estimated at 70 mph.
A large swath of hen egg sized hail fell across portions of Edendale Township.
The tornado damaged numerous trees in shelterbelts and snapped a few power poles along its path. Peak winds were estimated at 110 mph.
Large hail and strong winds produced widespread rooftop and crop damage in the Clifford area.
Debris from this tornado was visible on radar. The tornado snapped numerous trees in shelterbelts and partially debarked others. Peak winds were estimated at 120 mph.
A persistent wall cloud and funnel were observed.

The tornado crossed highway 11 and quickly became enshrouded in heavy rain and hail. Large tree branches were blown down in shelterbelts along its path. Peak winds were estimated at 80 mph.
The tornado was observed from Interstate 94, where a series of dust plumes were noted.
Winds also gusted up to 50 mph.
Large tree limbs and branches were blown down by the strong wind gusts.
Large tree branches were blown down in shelterbelts along Interstate 29 by the strong winds.

The tornado blew down an old barn and blew out two steel grain bins at one farmstead, snapped six pine trees at a second, and snapped several poplar trees at a third. Numerous trees were snapped and a steel grain bin was blown off its foundation at one farmstead. A neighboring farmstead also had numerous large branches blown down. Peak winds were estimated at 90 mph.

This tornado was partially engulfed in downburst winds and hail along its nearly 20 mile path. Large wooden power poles were snapped, roofing was stripped off of homes, steel pole sheds were totally dismantled, numerous steel grain bins were crushed, and large metal segments were carried for a mile or more downwind. Bean and grain fields were completely stripped. Peak winds were estimated at 120 mph.
Large portions of Alma and East Alma townships were stripped of small grain and bean crops by extreme downburst winds and wind driven hail.

This tornado and corresponding rear flank downdraft wind produced widespread dust, which greatly reduced the visibility. Numerous ash, poplar, cottonwood, and evergreen trees were snapped or uprooted in shelterbelts and groves along its path. Peak winds of 119 mph were measured by a mobile system.

This tornado snapped H-pole power poles, crushed steel grain bins, snapped numerous oak and ash trees, and toppled a barn along its path. Peak winds were estimated at 130 mph.

As it crossed into Polk County, it continued to damage numerous barns, sheds, and outbuildings along its path and was likely wrapped in downburst winds and rain. The tornado hit the town of Winger, where it damaged hundreds of trees, damaged the siding and roofs on many homes, and destroyed several grain bins.
Many small and large tree branches were blown down in town.

A cell phone tower was crumbled and bent to the ground and two satellite receiver dishes were destroyed. The roofs were ripped off of two tall grain storage bins. Peak straight line wind gusts were estimated at 90 to 100 mph.
The wind gusts were measured at the Fosston airport. The wind sensor lost power and stopped reporting, so the peak winds could have been higher.

The tornado was likely wrapped in downburst winds and rain at times.

This tornado was the third of five tornadoes in Grant County. The tornado tracked mainly over open fields and pasture land. A slight marking was noted in a field via video and a storm damage survey team. Peak winds were estimated at 70 mph.

This tornado was the fourth of five tornadoes in Grant County. The tornado crossed U. S. Highway 59 about two miles south of Elbow Lake, the south end of Pomme de Terre Lake, and the Tipsinah Mounds Golf Course. It snapped and uprooted numerous trees, several power poles, and ravaged corn fields. It tore down a small tower, roofing, and roof sections from homes and a golf course clubhouse. Peak winds were estimated at 115 mph.

This tornado was the fifth and southernmost of five tornadoes that occurred in Grant County. This tornado had a persistent wall cloud for several minutes prior to tornado development. The tornado quickly became wrapped in heavy rain. It snapped or uprooted several trees, and tore roofing off of a home and a pole shed before passing over highway 55, as confirmed by video and a storm damage survey. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph.

Initial report of a tornado on Lower Red Lake, which moved onshore at Red Lake and tracked for less than one mile. The tornado lifted by 515 PM CDT. Damaging downburst winds, heavy rain, and large hail continued to track southeastward with this storm. Damage was reported to the Tribal College, as well as other homes and buildings in the area. A light pole was snapped and several signs were toppled. Several large trees were snapped.

Hail up to tennis ball sized, as well as downburst winds of near 70 mph impacted the areas between the Communities of Red Lake and Redby, as well as the Tribal lands immediately south and southeast of these Communities. Widespread shingle and roofing damage was evident, along with home and vehicle windows shattered. Several large tree limbs blown down and large trees snapped.

This tornado formed near the shore of Lower Red Lake and tracked to the southeast. It crossed MN HWY 1 near the intersection with BIA15 and penetrated deeply into a large evergreen and oak forest. Trees were snapped and debris was tangled, though most debris tracked with the southeast moving storm. The tornado appeared to have dissipated around 522 PM CDT, after crossing BIA18, roughly 6 miles ESE of Redby.

This tornado was likely wrapped in downburst winds, heavy rain, and large ail. The tornado crossed several County and Township roads as it tracked to the southeast, with numerous poplar and oak trees snapped along it's path. It appears to have crossed portions of Dark Lake, Whitefish Lake, and Sandy Lake in Nebish and Hagali Townships, before dissipating. near the western edge of Gull Lake, about 4 WNW of Tenstrike.
